linear-search.simple: Linear search is the plainest way to find something: look at every item, one after another, until you see the one you want. Think of hunting for one sock in a drawer full of loose socks. You pick up a sock and check it. If it is the wrong one, you pick up the next. You stop when you find your sock, or when the drawer is empty. A computer does the same with a list: it starts at the first item, checks each in turn, and if it reaches the end without a match it reports that the item is not there. The method always works, and the list can be in any order. Its weakness is speed. A list twice as long can take twice as many checks. That is fine for a short list. It is too slow for a huge list that gets searched again and again.
linear-search.analogyTitle: A name on an unsorted sign-up sheet
linear-search.analogyText: Someone hands you a sign-up sheet where people wrote their names in the order they arrived. To find out whether Priya signed up, you put your finger on the first line and read down, one name at a time. Arrival order tells you nothing about where her name might be, so you cannot skip a line: the one you skip could be hers. If you see her name, you stop early. To say she is not on the sheet, your finger has to reach the bottom.
linear-search.limits: Your eye can take in several lines at a glance and may catch a familiar name before your finger gets there. The algorithm cannot: it examines exactly one item at a time, in order. A person might also remember roughly where a name was written. Linear search remembers nothing between one search and the next.

binary-search.simple: Binary search finds an item in a sorted list by cutting the list in half again and again. You already know the idea. To find a word in a paper dictionary, you do not start at page one. You open the book near the middle and look at a word. If your word comes later in the alphabet, you can ignore the whole first half. If it comes earlier, you can ignore the second half. Then you do the same with the half that is left. Each look throws away half of the remaining pages, so the pile shrinks very fast. A list of a thousand items needs about ten looks. A list of a million needs only about twenty. There is one firm condition: the list must already be in order. If it is not, a look at the middle tells you nothing about which half to keep, and the method can give wrong answers.
binary-search.analogyText: A friend picks a whole number from 1 to 100 and answers each guess with "higher", "lower" or "correct". Guess 50. If the answer is "higher", the number is somewhere from 51 to 100, so guess the middle of that range. Keep guessing the middle of whatever range is left. Each answer removes half of the remaining numbers, and seven guesses are always enough, whatever number was picked.
binary-search.limits: In the game the number is always there. A list might not contain the target, so the search must also notice when the range has shrunk to nothing. The game also uses every number from 1 to 100 with no gaps. A real list has gaps, so binary search halves the range of positions, not the range of values, and looks at whatever value sits in the middle position. Last, your friend can answer about any guess at once. A computer can do that only if it is able to jump straight to any position in the list.

bubble-sort.simple: Bubble sort is a way to put a list in order, such as arranging numbers from smallest to largest. It may be the simplest method there is. Look at the first two items. If they are in the wrong order, swap them. Then look at the second and third items and do the same. Keep going until you reach the end of the list. That is one pass. During a pass, the biggest item gets carried all the way to the end, a little like a bubble rising to the top of a glass. Now make another pass, and the next biggest item settles beside it. Repeat until a whole pass goes by without a single swap. That means every item is in order with its neighbour, so the list is sorted. Bubble sort is easy to follow but slow on long lists. People learn it first, and then learn why other methods are faster.
bubble-sort.analogyTitle: A row of people trading places by height
bubble-sort.analogyText: People stand in a row in any order. Starting at the left, each person compares heights with the neighbour on their right, and the two trade places if the taller one is on the left. Now follow two people. The tallest person wins every comparison, so a single walk along the row carries them all the way to the right-hand end. The shortest person, if they start at the right-hand end, is less lucky: each walk gives them one trade, so they move only one place to the left per walk. That slow traveller is why a row can need many walks. When a whole walk happens with nobody trading places, the row is in height order.
bubble-sort.limits: In a real row, many pairs could trade places at the same moment, and anyone can glance along the row and see who is badly out of place. Bubble sort checks one pair at a time and never looks further than the next neighbour.

selection-sort.simple: Selection sort is a way to put a list in order, such as arranging numbers from smallest to largest. It works the way many people tidy a shelf. Look through the whole list and find the smallest item. Move it to the front by trading places with whatever was there. That first spot is now finished. Next, look through the rest of the list and find the smallest item that is left. Trade it into the second spot. Keep going, one spot at a time, until every spot holds the right item. To find the smallest item, the method checks every remaining item in turn and remembers the smallest it has seen so far. It does all of that checking even when the list was already in order, so it is slow on long lists. Its strength is that it moves items very rarely: at most one trade for each spot.
selection-sort.analogyText: To arrange a shelf of books from shortest to tallest, run your finger along the whole shelf, find the shortest book, and swap it with the book at the left-hand end. From then on the shelf has two parts. On the left are the books already in place, in order and never touched again. On the right are the rest. Each sweep covers only the right-hand part and moves one more book across the line, so the sweeps get shorter as the shelf fills in.
selection-sort.limits: A person can spot the shortest book on a shelf at a glance. A computer cannot glance: it has to look at every remaining book, one at a time, on every sweep. A person would also remember which books were nearly the shortest. Selection sort forgets everything it learned in a sweep except the one winner, and starts the next sweep from nothing.

insertion-sort.simple: Insertion sort is a way to put a list in order, and it is how most people sort a hand of playing cards. Pick up the cards one at a time. The first card is in order by itself. Take the second card and put it before or after the first, whichever is right. Take the third card and slide it into the right place among the first two. Carry on like this. Each new card goes into its correct place among the cards you already hold, so the cards in your hand are always in order. When there are no cards left to pick up, the whole hand is sorted. This method is quick when the list is short. It is very quick when the list is almost in order already, because each item is then close to where it belongs. On a long, jumbled list it is slow, because items have to travel a long way.
insertion-sort.analogyTitle: One card going into a sorted hand
insertion-sort.analogyText: Look closely at a single card going in. You hold a few cards in your left hand, already in order, and pick up one more. You look along the held cards from the right, largest first, and stop at the first one that is not larger than the new card. The new card slides in just after it. If the new card is larger than everything you hold, one look settles it. If it is the smallest, you look at every card in your hand.
insertion-sort.limits: With real cards, opening a gap is a single motion of the fingers. In a list stored in a computer, there is no free space between items: every larger value has to be copied one place to the right, one at a time, and that copying is where most of the time goes. A real card player also finds the place at a glance. The algorithm has no glance and compares one card after another.

merge-sort.simple: Merge sort is a way to put a list in order by splitting one big job into smaller jobs. It rests on one easy trick. Suppose you have two piles of cards, and each pile is already in order. You can combine them into a single ordered pile quickly. Look at the top card of each pile, take the smaller one, and repeat until both piles are gone. That is called merging. Merge sort uses this trick again and again. Cut the list in half. Cut each half in half, and keep cutting until every piece is a single item. A single item is already in order. Now merge the pieces in pairs to make ordered pieces of two. Merge those to make ordered pieces of four, and carry on until one ordered list remains. Merge sort does about the same amount of work whatever order the list starts in, so no input can catch it out.
merge-sort.analogyTitle: A stack of exam papers and two helpers
merge-sort.analogyText: A teacher has a tall stack of exam papers to sort by student name. The teacher splits the stack in two and hands each half to a helper with one request: bring it back sorted. When the two sorted stacks come back, combining them is easy. Look at the top paper of each stack, move whichever name comes first onto a new stack, and repeat. Nobody ever looks below the top of a stack. Each helper does the same with their own half: split it, hand the halves on, and merge what comes back. The handing-on stops when someone is given a single paper, which is already sorted.
merge-sort.limits: The desk in this picture has room for a third stack. A computer has to set that room aside: merge sort needs spare memory as large as the list it is sorting. The helpers in the picture also work at the same time, while the algorithm on this page finishes one half completely before it starts the other.

quick-sort.simple: Quick sort is a way to put a list in order, such as arranging numbers from lowest to highest. It works by picking one item from the list and asking the same question of every other item: are you smaller or bigger than this one? Smaller items go to one side. Bigger items go to the other side. The item you picked is now sitting in exactly the right spot, and it never has to move again. Then you do the same thing inside each side. The groups keep getting smaller until each one holds a single item. At that point the whole list is in order. Computers sort lists all day long: names, prices, scores, search results. Quick sort matters because, on most lists, it gets the job done with very little work. It turns slow when the picked item keeps turning out to be among the smallest or biggest in its group.
quick-sort.analogyTitle: Sorting a class by height with one volunteer
quick-sort.analogyText: Ask one student to stand still. Everyone shorter moves to their left, everyone taller to their right. That student is now standing in exactly the right place in the final line, even though neither group is sorted yet. Repeat inside each group with a new volunteer, and keep going until every group is a single person. How quickly this ends depends on the volunteers. A volunteer of middling height splits a group into two smaller ones. A volunteer who is the shortest or tallest of the group leaves everyone else in one group, and if that happens every time, each round places only one person.
quick-sort.limits: A class can shuffle around all at once, with everyone checking their height against the volunteer at the same moment. A computer running quick sort checks one item at a time. That is why we measure its work by counting comparisons.

heap-sort.simple: Heap sort is a way to put a list in order by picking out the biggest item again and again. Finding the biggest item in a jumbled list is slow, because you have to look at every item. Heap sort avoids that by first arranging the items in a pattern called a heap. Picture a chart like a family tree. One item sits at the top, two sit below it, two below each of those, and so on. The rule is that every item is at least as big as the two items directly below it. With that rule, the biggest item is always at the top. Heap sort takes the top item and puts it at the back of the list, where it belongs. Then it repairs the chart, which takes only a few steps, because only one path from top to bottom needs fixing. Now the next biggest item is at the top. Take it, repair, and repeat until nothing is left.
heap-sort.analogyTitle: Finding the runner-up in a knockout tournament
heap-sort.analogyText: After a knockout tournament everyone knows the champion. To find the second-best player there is no need to play the whole tournament again: the runner-up must be someone the champion beat, and that is only one player per round. A heap works in a similar way. Once the largest value has been taken from the top, only the values along a single path from top to bottom need to be compared to find the next largest. For a thousand values that is about ten levels, not a thousand checks.
heap-sort.limits: A tournament bracket writes every player at the bottom and copies winners upward, so names appear several times. A heap stores each value once and promises less: only that a parent is at least as large as its children. Two values on different branches are in no known order. A heap also needs no bracket drawn anywhere. It is just the list itself, read with a rule that says which positions count as children of which.

counting-sort.simple: Counting sort puts a list in order without asking which of two items is bigger. It works when the items are whole numbers from a small range, such as exam marks from 0 to 100. Imagine sorting a big pile of exam papers by mark. Draw a tally chart with one row for each possible mark. Go through the pile once and add a tally for each paper. Now you know how many papers got each mark. From that you can work out where every group belongs in the finished pile. If three papers scored 0 and five scored 1, then the papers that scored 2 must start at the ninth place. Go through the pile a second time and put each paper straight into its place. This is very fast when the range of marks is small. It is wasteful when the range is huge, because the chart needs a row for every possible value, whether or not any paper has it.
counting-sort.analogyText: A sorting office has a wall of pigeonholes, one for each delivery district, arranged in order. A clerk picks up each letter, reads its district number, and drops it into that pigeonhole. No letter is ever held up against another letter. When the sack is empty, walking along the wall from the first hole to the last collects the letters in district order. The wall works because the districts are few. A hole for every possible phone number would fill the building with empty holes, and walking past them all would take longer than sorting the letters any other way.
counting-sort.limits: A pigeonhole can hold any number of letters, but a block of computer memory cannot stretch. That is why counting sort makes a counting pass first: it has to know how much room each value needs before it writes anything.

hash-table.simple: A hash table stores things so that you can find any one of them almost at once, without searching through the rest. Think of a cloakroom with a row of numbered hooks. When you hand in a coat, the attendant uses a fixed rule to turn your ticket number into a hook number, and hangs the coat there. When you come back, the same rule gives the same hook, so the attendant walks straight to it. Sometimes the rule sends two tickets to the same hook. The version in this lesson handles that simply: if the hook is taken, try the next hook along, then the next, until one is free. To find a coat later, start at its hook and walk along in the same way until you see it. If you reach an empty hook first, the coat is not there. This works well while plenty of hooks are free. As the rack fills, taken hooks bunch together and the walks get longer.
hash-table.analogyTitle: Assigned parking on a ring road
hash-table.analogyText: Every resident of a circular street has an assigned parking space worked out from their house number. If someone else is already in your space, you drive on and take the next free one. Because the street is a ring, driving past the last space brings you round to the first. To find a neighbour's car, go to their assigned space and walk forward from there. You will reach the car before you reach a gap, because when they parked there was no gap between their assigned space and the one they took. That is why an empty space proves the car is not on the street.
hash-table.limits: On a real street cars drive away and leave gaps. In the table a gap means "stop looking", so an item that is removed must leave a marker behind, or items parked beyond it would be lost. And the rule that assigns places, called the hash function, does not follow house numbers along the street: a good one scatters items so that similar ones land far apart.

union-find.simple: Union-find keeps track of which things belong to the same group while groups keep merging. Picture a school where friend circles form over time. At first every student is alone. Whenever two students become friends, their two circles join into one. At any moment you may want to ask: are these two students in the same circle? Union-find answers that quickly. Each circle has one member who acts as its captain. Every other student remembers just one person in the circle, someone a step closer to the captain. To find your captain, you ask that person, who asks theirs, and so on, until the chain reaches the captain. Two students are in the same circle exactly when they reach the same captain. To merge two circles, one captain simply starts pointing to the other. Two small habits keep these chains short, so even with millions of students each question takes only a few steps.
union-find.analogyText: Every employee knows one thing: who their boss is. Nobody holds a list of who works for which company. To learn which company someone belongs to, follow the chain of bosses up to the one person with no boss, the chief executive. When two companies merge, one chief executive starts reporting to the other. Nothing else changes and nobody else is told, yet every chain that ended at the old chief executive now runs on to the new one. In that single change everyone below has joined the bigger company.
union-find.limits: In a real company the chain of bosses means something. Here the links are bookkeeping and nothing else: who points to whom says nothing about the items except which group they are in. That is why the structure is free to rearrange itself, pointing everyone it passes straight at the top, which no real organisation would do. Real companies can also split up again. Union-find cannot undo a merge.

bfs.simple: Breadth-first search is a way to explore a network of connected things, one layer at a time. Think of a rumour spreading through a school. On day one, a single student knows it. On day two, all of that student's friends know. On day three, the friends of those friends know, and so on. Breadth-first search explores in the same order. It starts at one point. It visits everything one step away, then everything two steps away, then three. To keep that order straight, it uses a waiting line. Each newly found point joins the back of the line, and the next point to explore always comes from the front. Because it works outward in layers, the first time it reaches a point, it has found a route there with the fewest possible steps. That is why it can find the shortest way through a maze, or the smallest number of introductions that connect two people.
bfs.analogyTitle: Ripples from a stone dropped in a pond
bfs.analogyText: Drop a stone into still water and a ring spreads outward. Everything inside the ring has been reached and nothing beyond it has. The ring reaches nearby points first and distant points later, and it never skips ahead. In breadth-first search the waiting line plays the part of the ring. The points in the line are the outer edge of what has been found so far, and exploring from the front of the line pushes that edge outward one step at a time.
bfs.limits: A ripple touches every point on a ring at the same moment. The algorithm visits one point at a time, taking them in the order of the line. A ripple also travels real distance, while the search only counts steps: a long road and a short road each count as one. When the lengths matter, the picture is still right but the algorithm must change to Dijkstra's.

dfs.simple: Depth-first search is a way to explore a network of connected places. It follows one route as far as it goes before trying another. Think of exploring a maze. You walk forward, and at every junction you take a passage you have not tried yet. You keep going until you reach a dead end or a place you have already been. Then you walk back to the last junction that still has an untried passage, and take it. To avoid going round in circles, you mark each place the first time you step into it. To find your way back, you remember the route you came by. When you have backed all the way out to the start and no untried passage is left, you have visited every place that can be reached. Computers use this method to solve puzzles, to find loops in a network, and to work out which jobs must be done before others.
dfs.analogyTitle: Exploring a maze with a ball of string
dfs.analogyText: Take two things into the maze: a ball of string and a piece of chalk. Tie the string at the entrance and unwind it as you walk, and chalk a mark at every junction you enter. The chalk answers one question: have I been here before? The string answers another: how do I get back to the last junction? At any moment the string traces the route from the entrance to where you stand, and winding it back one junction is how you back up. In the algorithm the string is called the stack, and the chalk marks are the record of places already discovered.
dfs.limits: A person in a maze can see down a corridor and guess which way looks promising. The algorithm has no such sense: it tries passages in whatever order they are listed. The string shows a way back to the entrance, not the shortest way. A place right next to the entrance may be reached only at the end of a long winding route.

topological-sort.simple: Topological sorting puts a set of jobs in an order that obeys every "this before that" rule. Think of getting dressed. Socks go on before shoes. Trousers go on before a belt. A shirt goes on before a jacket. No single rule gives you the whole order, but together they forbid many orders. Here is a way to find one that works. Look for a job that is waiting for nothing, and do it. Cross off every rule that starts with that job. Some other jobs may now be waiting for nothing, so they are ready too. Keep doing a ready job and crossing off its rules until every job is done. If you get stuck with jobs left over, the rules must go round in a circle, such as A before B and B before A. Then no order can work. Computers use this method to decide which files to build first and which spreadsheet cells to calculate first.
topological-sort.analogyText: A course catalogue lists which courses must be passed before others. To plan a degree, write down any course with no prerequisites, then cross it off the prerequisite lists of the other courses. Some of those now have empty lists, so they become available. Often several courses are available at once. Any of them can go next, and each choice leads to a different plan that still obeys the catalogue. The method finds a valid order, not the only one. If two courses each list the other as a prerequisite, neither ever becomes available, and the catalogue has a mistake.
topological-sort.limits: A student can take several courses in the same term. The algorithm writes one line, a single course at a time, so its answer says nothing about how to finish in the fewest terms. Real prerequisites can also be waived or satisfied in alternative ways. The algorithm treats every rule as absolute.

dijkstra.simple: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the cheapest way to get from one place to every other place on a map. Picture towns joined by roads, where each road has a cost, such as minutes of driving. You start at home, which costs nothing to reach. Then you look for the nearest town you have not finished with. Nothing closer is left, so you already know the cheapest way to get there. Mark that town as finished. Next, check each road leading out of it. If going through this town gives a cheaper way to reach a neighbour, write down the new, lower cost. Now repeat: pick the nearest unfinished town, finish it, update its neighbours. When every town is finished, you know the cheapest cost to reach each one, and the route that gets you there. The method relies on one condition: no road may have a negative cost. Phones use this idea to plan journeys. The internet uses it to decide where to send data.
dijkstra.analogyText: Build the map out of pipes, each as long as its road is costly, and pour water in at the starting town. The water front reaches each junction at a time equal to its cheapest cost from the start, and it reaches the junctions in order of that cost, nearest first. Dijkstra's algorithm follows the front. Finishing the nearest unfinished town is the water arriving there. Water still on its way along other pipes cannot arrive any sooner, which is why that town's cost is final.
dijkstra.limits: Real water flows down every pipe at once. The algorithm deals with one junction at a time, so it needs a waiting list, called a priority queue, to tell it which junction comes next. The picture also assumes every pipe has a real length. A road with a negative cost has no meaning for water, and it breaks the algorithm too.

bellman-ford.simple: The Bellman-Ford algorithm finds the cheapest route from one place to every other place on a map. It still works when some roads have a negative cost, meaning that travelling the road earns you something back. Picture a delivery driver. Most roads cost fuel, but one road has a paying job on it. The method is patient. Write zero next to the start and "unknown" next to every other place. Then go through the whole list of roads. For each road, ask one question: does taking this road reach its far end more cheaply than the best known so far? If it does, write down the lower cost. One sweep through the list is not enough, because a new low cost in one place can lead to new low costs further on. So sweep again, until a whole sweep changes nothing. If the costs never stop falling, some loop of roads pays you every time you drive round it. Then no cheapest route exists, and the method says so.
bellman-ford.analogyTitle: Towns passing on news of a cheaper route
bellman-ford.analogyText: Every town keeps a signpost showing the cheapest known cost of reaching it from the capital. Once a day, each town tells its neighbours: "you can be reached through me for my cost plus the road between us." A town that hears a better offer than its signpost shows repaints the sign. News of a cheap route spreads one road further each day. If the map has V towns, any sensible route uses at most V − 1 roads, so after V − 1 days every signpost is right.
bellman-ford.limits: In the story every town speaks at the same moment, and news moves exactly one road per day. The algorithm on this page checks roads one at a time in a fixed order and uses each new number immediately, so in one pass good news can travel along several roads if they happen to be listed in a helpful order. That is why it often finishes early. The story also has no ending when a loop of roads pays out: the towns would repaint their signs for ever. The algorithm stops after V − 1 passes and uses one more scan to detect the loop.

a-star.simple: A* (say "A star") is a way to find the shortest route to a goal without wasting time searching in the wrong directions. Imagine crossing a city on foot toward a tall tower you can see in the distance. At every street corner you could ask two things. How far have I walked to get here? And how far does it still look to the tower? Add the two numbers, and you have a guess at the length of a whole trip through that corner. A* keeps a list of corners it could explore next, and it always picks the one with the smallest total. Corners that lead away from the tower get large totals, so they wait at the bottom of the list. Many are never explored at all. If the "how far does it look" guess never says the goal is farther than it really is, the route A* finds is truly the shortest. Video games use it to move characters, and robots use it to plan their paths.
a-star.analogyTitle: The straight line to the tower
a-star.analogyText: The guess at each corner is the straight-line distance to the tower. Streets may force detours, so the real walk is at least that long, never shorter. That makes the total at a corner, the distance walked so far plus the straight-line distance remaining, the best case for any route through that corner. The real trip may turn out longer than the total, but never shorter. So once A* has reached the tower, and no corner left on its list has a best case below the length of the route it found, nothing still unexplored could beat it.
a-star.limits: A walker stands in one place and must walk back to try a different street. A* does not walk. It keeps a list of every corner it could continue from and jumps to whichever is most promising, at no cost. The picture also assumes your eye judges the distance correctly. If your estimate is too high, A* may settle for a route that is not the shortest. And if you cannot see the tower at all, the estimate is useless and A* has to search in every direction.

minimax.simple: Minimax is how a computer chooses a move in a game for two players, such as noughts and crosses or chess. It looks ahead. It imagines each move it could make, then each reply the other player could make, then its own answers to those, and so on. At the end of every imagined line of play it writes down a score: high if the game went well for the computer, low if it went badly. Then it works backwards. On its own turns it assumes it will pick the move with the highest score. On the other player's turns it assumes they will pick the move with the lowest score, the one that is worst for the computer. The move that still comes out best is the one it plays. There is also a shortcut, called alpha-beta pruning. Once one reply shows that a move is worse than a move already found, the computer stops looking at that move. Its other replies no longer matter. The shortcut never changes the answer. It only saves work.
minimax.analogyTitle: Choose a bag, and a rival picks what you get from it
minimax.analogyText: Three bags sit on a table. You choose a bag, and then a rival, who wants you to get as little as possible, takes one thing out of it and hands it to you. To choose well you look into each bag and find its worst item, because that is the one you will be given. Then you take the bag whose worst item is best. That is minimax. Now the shortcut. Say the worst thing in the first bag is worth 4. You open the second bag and the first thing you see is worth 2. You can close that bag at once. Your rival would hand you that item or something worse, and you already have a bag that guarantees 4. Whatever else is in the second bag makes no difference.
minimax.limits: A bag is one choice deep. A game goes many turns deep, with you and your rival choosing in turn, so each item in a bag is itself a bag, and a limit found near the top of the tree is carried down to cut branches far below. The picture also assumes your rival always picks what is worst for you. A real opponent makes mistakes, and minimax does nothing to tempt them into one. And in a large game nobody can look into every bag: the search has to stop early and estimate.

q-learning.simple: Q-learning is a way for a computer to learn what to do by trying things and seeing what happens. Nobody tells it the rules. Picture a robot in a room it has never seen. Somewhere there is a prize, and somewhere a hole it can fall into. The robot keeps a notebook. For every spot in the room, and every direction it could step from that spot, the notebook holds one number: its guess at how well things will turn out if it steps that way. At first every guess is zero. The robot wanders. When a step wins the prize, it raises the number for that step. When a step lands in the hole, it lowers it. And here is what makes it work. When a step only leads to a spot that already has a good number, part of that goodness is copied back to the step. So good numbers spread, one step at a time, from the prize back to the start. In the end the robot follows the biggest number from each spot. Now and then it still tries a random step, in case a better way exists.
q-learning.analogyTitle: Signposts in a park with no map
q-learning.analogyText: You walk in a large park with no map, looking for the café. At every junction stands a signpost with one space for each path. The only thing you may ever do is read the signpost where you have arrived, then write one number on the signpost you just left. A path that reaches the café earns a high number. A path that reaches a junction whose best number is already high earns a slightly lower one. Nobody ever sees the park from above, yet after enough walks the highest number at each junction points the way to the café.
q-learning.limits: A person would remember the whole walk and start to picture the map. Q-learning keeps nothing except the numbers and changes one of them per step, which is why it is slow: one walk moves what has been learned back by a single junction. The picture also hides the gamble at every junction, between following the best number and trying a path whose number is low or blank, which is the only way to find out that a signpost is wrong. And a park stays put. If the same path could lead to different places on different days, each number would have to become an average over many tries.

kruskal.simple: Kruskal's algorithm finds the cheapest way to connect a set of places so that you can get from any one of them to any other. Imagine several villages with no roads between them. An engineer has a list of roads that could be built, each with a price. The villages want everyone to be able to reach everyone else, for the least money in total. The method is short. Sort the list from the cheapest road to the most expensive. Go down the list one road at a time. If a road joins two villages that cannot yet reach each other, build it. If they can already reach each other, even by a roundabout route, skip it, because it would cost money and connect nothing new. Stop when all the villages are linked. The surprise is that this works. Always taking the cheapest useful road, with no planning ahead, gives the cheapest possible network. Cheapest to build is not the same as most convenient to travel: two neighbouring villages may end up joined only by a long way round.
kruskal.analogyText: Swap the villages for islands and the roads for bridges. At the start every island is its own landmass. Each bridge that gets built fuses two landmasses into one, so the map is always a set of landmasses that only ever merge. The question to ask of the next cheapest bridge becomes simple: are its two ends on the same landmass? If not, build it. If so, it is a waste of money, so cross it off. When only one landmass is left, you are done.
kruskal.limits: The picture hides how the algorithm knows whether two islands are on the same landmass. Checking that quickly, many thousands of times, needs a data structure of its own, called union-find. And real engineers can do things the list does not allow, such as building a junction in open water. The algorithm only chooses among the bridges it is given.

pagerank.simple: PageRank is a way to measure how important each page is in a web of pages that link to one another. It was created to help a search engine decide which results to show first. The idea is that a link is a kind of vote. A page that many others link to is probably worth reading. But the votes are not equal. A link from an important page counts for more than a link from a page nobody visits. That sounds like a circle: to score one page, you need the scores of the others. The way out is to start by giving every page the same score. Then let each page share its score out along its links, and repeat. After enough rounds the scores stop changing.
pagerank.analogyText: Imagine someone browsing with no purpose at all. On each page they usually click one of its links, chosen at random. Now and then, with a fixed probability, they get bored and jump to a page picked at random from the whole web. Follow this surfer for a very long time and count the visits. The share of time spent on each page is its PageRank. Pages with many links pointing at them are visited often, and so are pages linked from those.
pagerank.limits: Real readers do not click at random. They read, search, follow some links far more than others, and use bookmarks. PageRank is not a measurement of traffic. It is a score computed from the links alone, and it knows nothing about what a page says or whether it is any good. The random jump is not a claim about behaviour either. It is there for a mathematical reason: without it, dead ends and closed loops of pages would trap the surfer, and the scores would not settle to a single sensible answer.

critical-path.simple: The critical path method works out how long a project must take and which jobs cannot be late. A project is a set of jobs, and some jobs have to wait for others. You cannot paint a wall before it is built. Jobs that do not wait for each other can be done at the same time by different people. So a project is usually much shorter than all of its jobs added together. What matters are the chains of jobs that must happen one after another. The longest chain sets the length of the whole project. It is called the critical path. If any job on it runs a day late, the whole project ends a day late. Jobs that are not on it have spare time, called slack. They can start a little late and nothing bad happens. Knowing this tells the person in charge where to watch closely and where there is room to breathe.
critical-path.analogyTitle: Cooking a dinner with several dishes
critical-path.analogyText: A roast needs 20 minutes of preparation and then 100 minutes in the oven. The vegetables need 10 minutes of chopping and 20 minutes of cooking. A sauce takes 15 minutes. Everything should be ready together. Dinner cannot be served sooner than 120 minutes after you begin, because the two steps of the roast must follow one another and together they take that long. That chain is the critical path. The vegetables and the sauce can each be started at any moment inside a wide window, and dinner is still on time. That freedom is their slack. Start the roast five minutes late, and dinner is five minutes late.
critical-path.limits: One cook has two hands. The method assumes that tasks which do not wait for each other can always run at the same time, as if there were enough cooks and burners for everything. It also treats every time as known exactly, while real tasks run over.

fibonacci-dp.simple: Dynamic programming is a way to stop a computer doing the same work twice. The Fibonacci numbers make a good first example. They start 0, 1, and after that each number is the sum of the two before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. Suppose you want the thirtieth one. One way is to say: I need the two numbers before it. For each of those, I need the two before them, and so on down. That works, but it asks for the same small answers again and again, millions of times in all. The cure is to work out each answer once and keep it. Then about thirty short sums are enough. The same habit, solving each small problem once and reusing the answer, speeds up many harder problems.
fibonacci-dp.analogyText: A pupil is asked the same long sum several times in one lesson. The first time, they work it out and write the answer in a notebook. Every later time, they read it off the page. The work is done once however often the question comes back. There are two ways to use the notebook. One is to write each answer down as the question comes up. The other is to know which questions are coming and work through them in order, easiest first, so that every answer needed is already on the page. For Fibonacci, that means starting from 0 and 1 and filling the page upward.
fibonacci-dp.limits: A notebook only helps when the same question really does come back, and when its answer cannot change between askings. It also takes up space: the page has one line for every different question.

lcs.simple: The longest common subsequence is the longest list of letters that appears in two pieces of text in the same order. The letters do not have to sit next to each other. Take STONE and LONGEST. Cross out letters from each word until what is left is the same in both. The most you can keep is ONE. That shared part is what the two texts have in common, and everything outside it is what changed. This is how a computer shows the difference between two versions of a document. It finds the lines that both versions share, in order, and marks the rest as removed or added. Trying every way of crossing out letters would take far too long. So the method fills in a grid. Each square answers the question for the first few letters of each word, using the answers in the squares beside it. The last square gives the answer for the whole words.
lcs.analogyTitle: Two playlists with songs in common
lcs.analogyText: Two friends each have a playlist. They want to listen together to as many songs as possible, playing them in an order that respects both lists. Each may skip songs, but neither may go backwards. The longest such run of shared songs is the longest common subsequence of the two playlists. The songs skipped on one list are deletions, and the songs skipped on the other are insertions.
lcs.limits: A playlist rarely contains the same song twice, and without repeats the problem is easier. Text repeats letters constantly, and each copy could be paired with any copy in the other string. The choice matters, because pairing one letter rules out pairings that would cross it. That is why the table is needed. Also, there is often more than one longest common subsequence, and the algorithm reports just one of them.

edit-distance.simple: Edit distance measures how different two pieces of text are. It counts the fewest small changes needed to turn one into the other. A small change means adding one letter, removing one letter, or swapping one letter for another. To turn CAT into CART you add an R, so the distance is 1. Spelling checkers use this idea. When you mistype a word, they look for real words that are only a change or two away from what you typed. Finding the fewest changes sounds hard, because there are so many ways to edit a word. The method here avoids trying them all. It starts with the easiest questions, about the first letter or two of each word. Then it works up to longer and longer beginnings of the two words, writing each answer in a grid. Each new answer needs only three answers already in the grid. The last square filled in is the distance between the whole words.
edit-distance.analogyTitle: Crossing a city grid with tolls
edit-distance.analogyText: Picture a grid of streets. You start at the top-left corner and must reach the bottom-right. Moving one block down means deleting a letter. Moving one block right means inserting a letter. Both cost one coin. You can also cut diagonally across a block: that is free if the two letters at that block match, and costs one coin if they differ. The edit distance is the fewest coins for the whole trip. The cheapest way to reach any corner is the cheapest of the three ways to arrive there, from above, from the left, or diagonally, so you can work out every corner in turn by sweeping across the grid.
edit-distance.limits: In this city every street is one-way: down, right, or diagonally down and right. That is why one sweep, row by row, is enough. On a real map with two-way streets you would need a method such as Dijkstra's algorithm. The picture also makes every toll one coin. Real typing errors are not all equally likely, and plain edit distance does not know that.

knapsack.simple: The knapsack problem is about choosing what to take when you cannot take everything. Picture a hiker with a bag that can hold only so much weight. Each thing she could pack has a weight and a value to her. Which things should go in the bag so that the total value is as high as possible and the bag is not too heavy? Each item is either taken whole or left behind. That is what the 0/1 in the name means. One tempting plan is to grab the items that give the most value for their weight. That plan can fail, because it may leave space that nothing else fits. Trying every possible selection always works, but the number of selections doubles with each extra item. The method here is smarter. It builds a grid of small questions: what is the best I can do with only the first few items and a smaller bag? Each answer comes from two answers already in the grid, one for leaving the newest item and one for taking it.
knapsack.analogyTitle: A packing notebook for every bag size
knapsack.analogyText: Suppose you kept a notebook that says, for every bag size up to yours, the best load you could make from the items looked at so far. A new item arrives. For each bag size you now have an easy question. Leave the item, and the notebook's old answer stands. Take it, and you get its value plus the notebook's old answer for a bag that is smaller by the item's weight, which is the room left for everything else. Write down the better of the two. After the last item, the entry for your real bag is the answer.
knapsack.limits: The notebook has one line per bag size, so it only works when weights are whole numbers and the capacity is not enormous. Real packing also involves shape and volume, and real items interact: a tent is worth little without its poles. The knapsack problem assumes one number for weight, one for value, and values that simply add up.

needleman-wunsch.simple: Needleman-Wunsch lines up two sequences of letters so that as many letters as possible match. Biologists use it to compare DNA or proteins from different living things. DNA can be written as a long string of four letters: A, C, G and T. Over millions of years, copies of the same gene drift apart. A letter changes here. A few letters go missing there. To see what two versions still share, you write one above the other and slide parts along, leaving gaps where letters were lost. Each matching pair of letters earns points. Each mismatched pair and each gap costs points. The best line-up is the one with the highest total. There are far too many line-ups to try them all. So the method fills in a grid. It works out the best score for the first few letters of each sequence, then for a few more, until the last square holds the best score for the whole thing. Walking back through the grid shows the line-up itself.
needleman-wunsch.analogyTitle: Two worn copies of the same manuscript
needleman-wunsch.analogyText: Two scribes copied the same text by hand, generations apart. Words were changed and whole lines were dropped. To compare the copies, you lay them side by side and slide lines down, leaving a blank wherever one copy seems to have lost something. An identical pair of lines is good, a differing pair is suspicious, and a blank is a loss. The arrangement you settle on is your best account of what the copyists did. Lining up two genes is the same exercise, with letters for lines and inheritance for the scribes.
needleman-wunsch.limits: A scholar comparing manuscripts uses meaning and judgement. The algorithm only adds up fixed scores, and the alignment with the best score is not guaranteed to be what actually happened. It also insists on lining up both sequences from the first letter to the last. If only a passage is shared, forcing the rest into line gives a misleading picture.

binomial-option-pricing.simple: An option is a ticket that lets you buy or sell something later, such as a share in a company, at a price fixed today. You may use the ticket or throw it away. Suppose a ticket lets you sell a share for 100 a year from now. If the share is then worth 80, the ticket gains you 20. If the share is worth 120, the ticket is useless and you ignore it. So what should the ticket cost today, when nobody knows the future price? This method draws a tree. From today's price the share can step up or step down. From each of those prices it can step up or down again, and so on until the last day. On the last day the ticket's worth is easy to see at every branch tip. Then you work backwards. The worth at each fork is a careful blend of the two worths that follow it. Fork by fork you arrive back at today, and the number you reach is the price of the ticket. It is the answer of a simplified model, not a promise about any real market.
binomial-option-pricing.analogyTitle: Labelling a trail map from the ends back to the start
binomial-option-pricing.analogyText: Imagine a trail that forks again and again, with a prize of known size at the end of every branch. You stand at the start and want to know what the walk is worth. Looking forward is confusing, because there are so many routes. Looking backward is easy. Write the prize at every trail end. Each last fork then needs only the two numbers just beyond it, blended into one. Once those forks are labelled, the forks before them have what they need, and so on back to the start. If the rules let you stop at a fork and take a fixed reward instead, compare that reward with the fork's blended number and write down the larger.
binomial-option-pricing.limits: On a trail map the blend could be a plain average. In the model the blending weights are forced by the sizes of the up and down moves and by the interest rate, and they are nobody's forecast. The map also has tidy forks at fixed places. A real price can jump any distance at any moment, and every real trade costs something, both of which the model leaves out.

euclidean-algorithm.simple: The Euclidean algorithm finds the largest number that divides two whole numbers exactly. That number is called their greatest common divisor. Here is a way to picture it. A floor is 48 units long and 18 units wide. You want to cover it with identical square tiles, as large as possible, without cutting any. What size should the tiles be? Start by laying the biggest squares the floor allows, 18 by 18. Two of them fit, and a strip 12 wide is left over. Now treat the strip the same way. One 12 by 12 square fits, and a smaller strip 6 wide is left. Squares of side 6 fill that last strip exactly, with nothing left. So 6 is the answer: tiles of 6 by 6 cover the whole floor. The method is more than two thousand years old. It is still in daily use, for example when computers create the keys that keep messages private.
euclidean-algorithm.analogyTitle: Measuring two sticks against each other
euclidean-algorithm.analogyText: You have a long stick and a short stick and want the longest ruler that measures both exactly. Lay the short stick along the long one as many times as it fits and mark what is left over. Any ruler that measures both sticks must measure that leftover piece too. So forget the long stick: the problem is now the short stick and the leftover. Repeat with those two. When a piece fits with nothing left over, that piece is the ruler.
euclidean-algorithm.limits: With real sticks the process might never end. The side and the diagonal of a square have no common measure at all, and the leftovers get smaller forever. The algorithm is about whole numbers, where each leftover is a smaller whole number and so the process must stop. The picture also suggests laying the stick down one length at a time, which is repeated subtraction. The algorithm does all of those subtractions at once with a single division.

sieve-of-eratosthenes.simple: The sieve of Eratosthenes finds all the prime numbers up to a limit you choose. A prime is a whole number bigger than 1 that cannot be divided evenly by anything except 1 and itself, such as 2, 3, 5 and 7. A kitchen sieve keeps what you want by letting everything else fall away, and this method does the same with numbers. Write down every number from 2 up to your limit. The first number, 2, is prime. Cross out every multiple of 2 after it: 4, 6, 8 and so on. Now move to the next number that is not crossed out. That is 3, so 3 is prime. Cross out its multiples. Keep going. Each time, the next number still standing is prime, and its multiples get crossed out. When you finish, the numbers left are exactly the primes. Nothing ever has to be divided. You only count along the list in equal steps.
sieve-of-eratosthenes.analogyTitle: Children sitting down in a line
sieve-of-eratosthenes.analogyText: Children wearing the numbers 2 to 100 stand in a line. The first child, number 2, stays standing and walks down the line asking every second child after them to sit: 4, 6, 8 and so on. Then the next child still standing, number 3, asks every third child after them to sit, and so it goes on. A child who is still standing when their turn comes has been passed over by every walker before them. Their number is not a multiple of any smaller prime, and that is enough to make it prime. When nobody new is left to take a turn, the children still standing are wearing exactly the prime numbers.
sieve-of-eratosthenes.limits: This picture is close to exact, so its weak points are the method's own. Some children are asked to sit more than once: number 12 hears it from 2 and again from 3. The computer wastes effort in the same way, and it is the main inefficiency of the method. There must also be one child for every number up to the limit. That is the real cost of the sieve: memory for the whole range. It is fine for a limit of a hundred or a hundred million, and impossible for numbers with hundreds of digits.

modular-exponentiation.simple: Fast modular exponentiation finds the remainder of a huge power without ever working out the huge power. Suppose you multiply 1,000 sevens together and want the remainder when the result is divided by 13. The full product has more than 800 digits. You do not need it. Two ideas get the answer using small numbers only. First, you may take the remainder after every multiplication and carry on from there. The final remainder comes out the same, and no number ever grows beyond 13 times 13. Second, you do not need 1,000 multiplications. Squaring a result doubles the count of sevens multiplied into it: 2, then 4, then 8, then 16. By mixing squarings with a few extra multiplications by 7, you can land on exactly 1,000 in fewer than twenty steps. The encryption that protects messages and payments online depends on this, using numbers hundreds of digits long.
modular-exponentiation.analogyTitle: A copier that can only double
modular-exponentiation.analogyText: You need a stack of exactly 13 sheets. Your machine has two buttons. One doubles the whole stack. The other adds a single sheet. Starting from 1 sheet: double and add one to get 3, double to get 6, double and add one to get 13. Three doublings, with an extra sheet twice, instead of adding one sheet twelve times. Which steps get the extra sheet is not a guess. It is read off 13 written in binary, 1101: after the leading 1, each digit means "double", and each 1 means "then add one".
modular-exponentiation.limits: The stack counts how many copies of the base have been multiplied together, which is the exponent, not the value of the power. Doubling the stack corresponds to squaring the running result, and adding a sheet corresponds to multiplying by the base once. The picture also leaves out the other half of the method: taking the remainder after every step, which is what keeps the numbers small.

bisection-method.simple: The bisection method finds the exact spot where something changes from too little to too much. Think of a shower dial. At one setting the water is too cold. At another setting it is too hot. Somewhere between the two is the setting that is just right. So you try the setting exactly halfway between. If the water is still too cold, the right setting must be in the upper half. If it is too hot, the right setting must be in the lower half. Either way, the gap you have to search is now half as wide. Try the middle of that gap, and halve it again. After ten tries the gap is about a thousand times narrower than at the start. After twenty tries it is a million times narrower. Computers use this to solve equations that no formula can solve. It is not the fastest method, but it is the safest. As long as the thing being measured changes smoothly, the answer can never slip out of the gap.
bisection-method.analogyText: Attach a number to each setting of the shower dial: how far the water is from comfortable. The number is below zero when the water is too cold, above zero when it is too hot, and exactly zero when it is right. Now the search has a precise form. You hold two settings, one where the number is negative and one where it is positive, and you want the setting where it is zero. The number at the halfway mark is negative or positive, and that sign alone says which half to keep. An equation is solved the same way. The unknown takes the place of the dial, and the expression that should equal zero takes the place of the comfort reading.
bisection-method.limits: A person at a shower uses more than "too hot" or "too cold". If the water is only slightly too cold, they nudge the dial a little instead of going to the halfway mark. Bisection ignores how far off the midpoint is and looks only at the sign, which is why faster methods exist. The dial also has one right setting, while the quantity in an equation can cross zero several times inside the gap. Bisection then finds one of the crossings and says nothing about the others.

newtons-method.simple: Newton's method solves an equation by making a guess and then improving it, quickly. Suppose you want an oven at exactly 200 degrees, and the dial has no numbers. You pick a position and wait. The oven settles at 180 degrees, which is 20 too low. You also know that, around this position, one notch of the dial adds about 10 degrees. So you turn it up 2 notches. That would be perfect if every notch added exactly 10 degrees. Real dials are not that regular, so you might land on 199. You measure again and make a much smaller correction. Each round uses two facts: how far off you are, and how quickly the result changes when the guess changes. Dividing the first by the second gives the correction. Once the guess is close, every round roughly doubles the number of correct digits, so a few rounds are enough. The catch is that a poor first guess can send the method the wrong way.
newtons-method.analogyTitle: A straight ramp laid along the curve
newtons-method.analogyText: Draw the problem as a curve. Along the ground are your possible guesses, and the height of the curve above or below each guess shows how far off it is. The answer is where the curve meets ground level. Stand on the curve at your current guess. Lay a long straight plank so that it touches the curve under your feet and points the way the curve is heading. Walk along the plank to the point where it reaches ground level. Then step straight up or down onto the curve again and lay a new plank. The plank is the oven-setter's assumption that the rate measured here holds all the way. If the curve is nearly straight between you and the answer, the first plank almost gets you there, and the second is aimed from much closer.
newtons-method.limits: A plank is straight and the curve is not. If the curve bends sharply between where you stand and the answer, the plank can point to a place farther away than where you started. If the curve is level under your feet, the plank is level too and never reaches the ground. And the picture hides the price: to lay the plank you must know the slope, which means having a formula for the derivative or computing an estimate of it.

euler-method.simple: Euler's method predicts the future one small step at a time. Suppose you know two things about a cup of hot tea: how warm it is now, and how fast it is cooling at this moment. What will its temperature be in one minute? A simple guess is to pretend the cooling rate stays the same for that minute. Multiply the rate by one minute and take that much off. Now you have a new temperature. Cooler tea cools more slowly, so you work out the new rate and repeat for the next minute. Step by step, you trace out the whole future of the tea. Many things in nature are like this. We know the rule for how fast they change, but there is no formula for where they end up. Planets, populations and electric circuits are examples. The smaller the steps, the closer the prediction stays to the truth, and the more steps it takes. With steps that are too big, the prediction can go badly wrong.
euler-method.analogyTitle: Navigating with only a compass and a speedometer
euler-method.analogyText: A ship out of sight of land cannot see where it is. The navigator knows the last marked position, the heading and the speed. So for the next hour the navigator draws a straight line on the chart in that direction, as long as the distance the ship would cover in an hour, and marks a new position at its end. Then the instruments are read again and the next line is drawn. The plotted course is a chain of straight segments standing in for the curved path of the real ship.
euler-method.limits: The ship's instruments measure the real ship, wherever it truly is. Euler's method computes the rate of change from its own estimated position. Once the estimate has drifted, the rates it uses belong to the wrong place, so errors can feed on themselves. A navigator also sights land sooner or later and corrects the chart. Euler's method never receives a correction: every error it makes is carried forward to the end.

runge-kutta-4.simple: Runge-Kutta is a careful way to predict the future one step at a time. Suppose you want to know where a rolling ball will be one second from now. The quick way is to check its speed now and pretend that speed holds for the whole second. But the ball may be slowing down, so the quick guess goes too far. The careful way takes four readings of the speed instead of one. The first is the speed right now. The second is the speed the ball would have half a second from now, if the first reading were right. The third is the speed at the half second again, using the second reading to get there. The fourth is the speed at the end of the second. Then the method averages the four, counting the two middle readings twice, and moves the ball by that average. Each step is four times the work. In return the answer is so much more accurate that far fewer steps are needed.
runge-kutta-4.analogyTitle: A navigator who checks the water ahead
runge-kutta-4.analogyText: A navigator plotting the next hour could draw one straight line using the current heading and speed. A more careful navigator treats that line as a trial. What would the wind and current be half an hour along it? Redraw using those, check the half-hour point again along the corrected line, then check the full-hour point. None of the trial lines is sailed. They exist to collect readings, and the course finally drawn blends all four, giving most weight to the two taken at the middle of the hour.
runge-kutta-4.limits: A real navigator cannot measure the sea at a place the ship has not reached. The method can make its trial readings only because the rule of change is a formula that can be evaluated for any time and any state, including states the system never visits. The weights are also not a navigator's judgement: they are fixed by algebra so that the errors of the four readings cancel as far as possible. And like Euler's method, RK4 never receives a correction from outside, so whatever error it makes is carried forward.

fft.simple: A Fourier transform takes a mixed-up signal and tells you what simple ingredients it is made of. Think of a chord on a piano. Three keys are pressed together, and the three notes travel through the air as one wobbling wave. A microphone records only that one combined wave. Yet your ear can tell that three notes are in it. A Fourier transform does the same job with arithmetic. It takes the recorded wave and reports how much of each pitch it contains: a lot of this note, some of that one, none of the others. The fast Fourier transform, or FFT, is a quick way to do that arithmetic. The plain way checks the recording against every possible pitch, one at a time, which is slow. The FFT splits the recording into halves again and again, and reuses the work that different pitches have in common. For a recording of about a thousand numbers, that is roughly two hundred times less work. That speed is why phones, audio software and medical scanners can use it constantly.
fft.analogyTitle: Hearing the notes in a chord
fft.analogyText: Nothing in the chord's combined wave is labelled with the names of the notes. A listener hears them anyway, because the ear responds to each pitch on its own. Picture a row of detectors, each tuned to a single pitch. Play the chord and three of them answer, each as strongly as its note is loud, while the rest stay quiet. A Fourier transform is that row of detectors done with numbers: one test for each pitch, and one answer from each, saying how much of that pitch is in the wave.
fft.limits: The ear listens continuously and judges pitch on its own scale. The FFT looks at one fixed block of samples and can only report on a fixed ladder of frequencies: 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on whole cycles per block. A note that falls between two rungs is smeared across several of them. The FFT also describes the block as a whole, so it cannot say when within the block a note began or ended.

gradient-descent.simple: Gradient descent is a way to find the lowest point of something when you cannot see all of it. Imagine standing on a hillside in thick fog. You want to reach the bottom of the valley. You cannot see the valley, but you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet. So you take a small step downhill. Then you feel the slope again and take another step. Keep going, and you end up somewhere low. Computers use the same trick with numbers. They start with a guess. They measure how wrong the guess is, and work out which small change would make it less wrong. They make that change, then repeat, often millions of times. This is what people mean when they say a computer program is learning: each step makes its answers a little less wrong.
gradient-descent.analogyTitle: The steepest way down, and the length of your stride
gradient-descent.analogyText: Two things about the foggy hillside still need saying. First, of all the directions that lead down, you step in the steepest one. Second, the length of your stride matters. Tiny strides are safe but slow. Giant strides can carry you clear across the valley and up the other side. In the algorithm the stride length is a number you choose, called the learning rate.
gradient-descent.limits: A hiker moves smoothly and would feel the ground begin to rise. The algorithm jumps from point to point and finds out where it has landed only afterwards. A hillside also has only two directions to move in, while the problems solved in machine learning have millions of directions at once. And fog or no fog, a hiker who reaches a small dip may be nowhere near the deepest valley. The algorithm has the same weakness.

simulated-annealing.simple: Simulated annealing is a way to search for the best answer when there are far too many possibilities to check them all. Picture a hiker in thick fog who wants the lowest point in a range of hills. A hiker who only ever walks downhill stops in the first dip they reach. A much deeper valley may lie just over the next ridge, and they will never see it. Simulated annealing lets the hiker walk uphill now and then. At each step the hiker picks a random spot nearby. If it is lower, they go there. If it is higher, they might still go, by chance. Early on they say yes to uphill steps often, so they roam widely and climb out of shallow dips. As time passes they grow stricter and say yes less and less. By the end they only walk downhill and settle into the low place they have found. The name comes from annealing: heating a metal and cooling it slowly, so that its atoms settle into an orderly pattern.
simulated-annealing.analogyTitle: A marble on a shaken tray
simulated-annealing.analogyText: Picture a tray moulded with many dents of different depths, and a marble that you want in the deepest dent without looking. If you hold the tray still, the marble rolls into the nearest dent and stays there. So you shake the tray. Hard shaking throws the marble out of any dent, shallow or deep. Then you shake more and more gently. There comes a stage where the shaking can still knock the marble out of a shallow dent but not out of a deep one, so the marble tends to collect in a deep one. When the shaking stops it rests there. The strength of the shaking is the temperature.
simulated-annealing.limits: A real marble rolls smoothly and carries momentum. The algorithm has neither: it proposes a jump, then accepts or refuses it by a rule of chance. The tray also suggests that patience always wins the deepest dent, and that is not true. With any cooling schedule fast enough to be practical, the search often ends in a good dent that is not the best one. And many real uses have no surface at all. The position is an arrangement, such as the order in which to visit cities, and a nearby point is the same arrangement with one small change.

genetic-algorithm.simple: A genetic algorithm searches for a good answer in the way a breeder improves animals or crops: by breeding from the best of each generation, not by designing the result. It starts with a crowd of random guesses at the answer to a problem. It scores every guess to see how good it is. Then it builds a new crowd. Good guesses are picked more often to be parents. Two parents are blended to make a child that takes after both. Now and then a child is changed a little at random, which brings in something new. The new crowd replaces the old one, and the cycle repeats. Over many rounds the crowd drifts toward better answers. Nobody tells it how to improve. It only needs a way to tell a better guess from a worse one. It does not promise the best answer, only a good one.
genetic-algorithm.analogyText: A plant breeder wants wheat that survives drought. Each season they grow a field of plants, see which ones cope best, and keep seed mostly from those. They cross promising plants with each other, hoping a child inherits the strengths of both. Now and then a seed carries a small accidental change, and once in a while that change helps. The breeder never works out what a drought-proof plant should look like. They only compare plants and decide which ones get to have offspring. After enough seasons the field looks very different from the first one.
genetic-algorithm.limits: The algorithm borrows three ideas from breeding and almost nothing else. Real inheritance works through genes in ways far more intricate than averaging two numbers. A breeder's field holds thousands of plants and takes a year per generation, while the algorithm uses a few dozen candidates and judges each by one fixed score. Natural evolution has no score and no goal at all. So a genetic algorithm is not a simulation of evolution, and nothing about biology guarantees that it will work on a given problem.

simplex.simple: The simplex method finds the best mix of things to make when several limits apply at once. Picture a bakery that sells bread and cakes. Cakes earn more money. But there are only so many cake tins, so much oven space and so many hours in the day. Every possible plan is a point on a map: so much bread across, so many cakes up. Each limit rules out part of the map with a straight line. What is left is a shape with flat sides and corners. Here is the key fact. If there is a best plan, one of the corners is a best plan. So there is no need to check the endless points inside the shape. The method starts at the corner where nothing is made. It looks along the edges that leave that corner and follows one that raises the profit. At the next corner it does the same again. When no edge leads to more profit, it stops. That corner is the best plan.
simplex.analogyTitle: Walking the fence of a sloping field
simplex.analogyText: A farmer's field lies on an even slope and is fenced with straight runs of fence. You want to stand at its highest point. Because the ground slopes evenly, the highest point cannot be in the middle of the field or partway along a fence: wherever you stand, you could go a little higher by walking uphill until a fence stops you, and then along that fence until a post stops you. So the highest point is at a fence post. Start at any post. Two fences leave it. If one of them climbs, follow it to the next post. Repeat. When both fences at your post lead downhill, you are at the top.
simplex.limits: A field has two directions and each post has two fences. A real problem with a thousand products is a shape in a thousand dimensions, with far more corners than could ever be listed and many edges at each one. Nobody can picture that shape, and the method never does: it works on a table of numbers, and the walk is only a way to understand what the table is doing. The slope must also be perfectly even. If the profit per item changes with the amount made, the best point need not be at a corner at all.

stochastic-gradient-descent.simple: Stochastic gradient descent is how a computer learns from a mountain of examples without looking at all of them before every move. Suppose a program should guess a house's price from its size, and it has a million past sales to learn from. It starts with a bad guessing rule. To improve the rule, it could check it against all million sales, work out the best small change, and make it. That is slow: a million checks for one small change. So it does something quicker. It picks a handful of sales at random, checks the rule on only those, and makes the small change they suggest. Then it picks another handful and does it again. Each handful gives a rough answer, a bit off in some random direction. But the handfuls are off in different directions, so over many steps the errors mostly cancel while the improvements add up. The word stochastic means random: chance decides which examples are used at each step.
stochastic-gradient-descent.analogyTitle: Asking ten customers instead of the whole town
stochastic-gradient-descent.analogyText: A baker wants to know whether the town would like the bread saltier or sweeter. Asking all 20,000 townspeople would give a reliable answer, once, after weeks. Instead the baker asks ten customers picked at random, changes the recipe slightly in the direction they favour, and asks ten different customers the next day. Any ten people can be unusual, so on some days the recipe moves the wrong way, but the unusual groups pull in different directions, and the recipe drifts toward what the town as a whole prefers. How many to ask is a choice. A hundred people each day give a steadier answer, but every day then costs ten times as much.
stochastic-gradient-descent.limits: The baker adjusts one thing. A model has many adjustable numbers, and each batch gives a direction for all of them at once. The baker could also stop when the customers seem content, but the batches in this method never agree: even at the best recipe, each small group still asks for some change, so the recipe keeps jittering unless the changes are made smaller over time. Last, the picture only works if the ten are chosen at random. A baker who only asks the early morning crowd ends up with bread for early risers, and a program that forgets to shuffle its data makes the same mistake.

adam.simple: Adam is a recipe for walking downhill when you can only feel the slope under your feet. Picture a hiker in fog, in a long, narrow valley. A plain walker takes big steps where the ground is steep and tiny steps where it is nearly flat. That goes badly here. The steep side walls throw the walker from side to side, while the gentle slope along the valley floor, the way that matters, earns only tiny steps. Adam adds two kinds of memory. First, it remembers which way the slope has pointed lately and steps in that averaged direction. Side-to-side slopes keep flipping, so they cancel. The slope along the valley keeps pointing the same way, so it adds up. Second, it keeps a separate memory for north-south and for east-west of how big the slopes have usually been, and divides by it. A direction with huge slopes gets its steps shrunk. A direction with tiny slopes gets its steps stretched. Computers use this recipe to train neural networks, which have millions of adjustable numbers instead of two directions.
adam.analogyText: Give the fog walker a notebook for each kind of memory. One holds the running average of recent slopes, which sets the direction. The other holds, separately for north-south and for east-west, how large the slopes have typically been, and the walker divides by it before stepping. Notice what that division does. On steep ground a large slope is divided by a large number. On gentle ground a small slope is divided by a small number. Either way the stride comes out about the same length. The walker covers ground at a similar pace in both directions, whatever the steepness.
adam.limits: No real walker can stride one length north-south and a different length east-west at the same moment. Adam can, because it treats every adjustable number on its own. That is also where the picture gives a warning: the adjustment works along the compass directions only. If the valley runs diagonally, both compass directions see the same mixture of steep and gentle slopes, and the separate strides help much less. The memory has a cost too. Carried by its averaged direction, the walker goes past the lowest point and has to turn back.

linear-regression.simple: Linear regression is a way to draw the best straight line through a scatter of dots. Suppose you write down how tall each of your classmates is and how big their shoes are. Put one dot on a chart for every person. The dots form a rough, sloping cloud, because taller people tend to have bigger feet. No straight line passes through every dot, so which line is the best one? The usual answer goes like this. For each dot, measure how far above or below the line it sits. Multiply each of those gaps by itself, so that big misses count for a lot. Then add them all up. The best line is the one with the smallest total. A computer can find it by starting with any line and nudging it, a little at a time, in whichever way makes the total smaller.
