Once you have the line, you can use it to make a sensible guess about someone new. Give it a height, and it reads off a shoe size.
linear-regression.analogyText: Pin every data point to the chart. Attach a spring from each pin straight up or down to a stiff rod, and let go. Each spring pulls the rod toward its own pin, and a spring stretched twice as far stores four times the energy. The rod swings and slides until the pulls balance. That resting position is the best line described above, known as the least squares line: it is the position with the least total energy in the springs, and spring energy grows with the square of the stretch. The springs also show the method's weak spot. One pin placed far from the others stretches its spring so much that it drags the whole rod toward itself.
linear-regression.limits: The springs in this picture can only stretch straight up and down, which no real spring would do without a guide rail. The method measures vertical gaps on purpose, because it is predicting y from x. And the rod settles somewhere even when the pins follow a curve, so a resting position is no evidence that a straight line was the right shape to use.

knn.simple: k-nearest neighbours is a way to label something new by looking at the labelled things most similar to it. Imagine a map of a town where every house is marked with the football team that family supports. A new family moves in, and you want to guess their team. A sensible guess is to look at the few houses closest to theirs and see which team most of them support. That is the whole method. The letter k is just the number of neighbours you ask. Ask only one, and a single odd household can fool you. Ask five and take the majority, and the guess is steadier. Ask the whole town, and you only learn which team is most popular overall. Computers use the same idea with measurements in place of streets. A fruit can be described by its weight and its colour. Two fruits with similar numbers sit close together on a chart, and a new fruit gets the label that most of its nearest neighbours carry.
knn.analogyText: Notice what you never had to do in that town. You did not need a theory of why people support the teams they do. You did not need to study the town beforehand or boil it down to any rule. You kept the map, and when a new family arrived you walked to the k houses nearest theirs and counted. Everything the method knows is the map itself, and all of its work happens at the moment a question is asked.
knn.limits: On a street map, distance has an obvious meaning and only two directions matter. Real data may have dozens of measurements in different units, such as grams and centimetres, and then the answer depends on how each one is scaled. With very many measurements, almost every point is far from every other, and the "nearest" neighbours are hardly nearer than the rest. The picture also hides the cost: to be sure which houses are nearest, the plain method measures the distance to every house in town, every time a new family arrives.

k-means.simple: k-means is a way to sort things into groups when nobody has told you what the groups are. Imagine a town that wants to put up three notice boards, so that everyone lives close to one of them. Where should they go? Start by putting the boards anywhere. Each household then picks the board nearest to it, which splits the town into three groups. Now move each board to the middle of the group that picked it. Some households will find that a different board has become their nearest, so they switch. Move the boards again, and keep going. After a few rounds nobody switches, and you stop. The boards now mark the centres of three neighbourhoods. Computers do the same with any kind of measurement, not only positions on a map. They can group customers with similar shopping habits, or the colours in a photograph. The letter k stands for the number of groups, and you have to choose it yourself.
k-means.analogyText: Watch one round at the notice boards and ask who gains. When a household switches to a board that has become nearer, its own walk gets shorter. When a board moves to the middle of the households that chose it, that group as a whole is better served than before. Neither move ever makes things worse, so the town cannot go round in circles. Sooner or later a round passes in which no household switches, and that is where the method stops. Nobody had to define the neighbourhoods in advance.
k-means.limits: A real board cannot stand in the middle of a lake, but a centroid is a plain average and can land where there are no points at all. Households would measure distance along streets; the method uses straight-line distance and squares it, so a few far-away households pull a board strongly. The town also has to decide the number of boards before it starts, and the method will carve out that many neighbourhoods whether or not the town really has them. Finally, a bad first placement can leave two boards sharing one neighbourhood while another neighbourhood has to share a single board with its neighbour, and the procedure will not notice.

pca.simple: Principal component analysis finds the directions in which a set of measurements varies most. Suppose you measure the height and the arm span of everyone in a school. Tall pupils tend to have long arms, so the two numbers mostly rise and fall together. Plot each pupil as a dot, with height across and arm span up, and the dots form a long thin cloud running diagonally. The long way along that cloud is the first principal direction. You could call it overall size. One number, how far along the cloud a pupil sits, tells you most of what the two measurements told you. The short way across the cloud is the second direction. It holds what is left over, such as arms that are unusually long for a pupil's height. The method finds these directions by arithmetic alone. Nobody tells it what size means. It earns its keep when there are not two measurements but fifty. Often a handful of directions hold nearly all the variation, and the rest can be dropped with little lost.
pca.analogyTitle: The shadow that shows the most
pca.analogyText: Hold a fork between a lamp and a wall and turn it. End-on, its shadow is a small blob that could be anything. Side-on, the shadow is long and you can count the prongs. A shadow is a flattened copy of an object: three dimensions pressed into two. Principal component analysis chooses the angle that makes the shadow of a cloud of points as spread out as possible, on the grounds that the most spread-out shadow keeps the points furthest apart and so loses the least.
pca.limits: The widest shadow is not always the one that shows what you care about. Two kinds of point can differ in a direction where the cloud is thin, and the widest shadow would press them together. A lamp also flattens three dimensions to two, while the method goes from any number of measurements to any smaller number, which no picture can show. And a cloud that is bent like a horseshoe has no flat shadow that does it justice, because the method can only choose a straight direction to look along.

logistic-regression.simple: Logistic regression is a way to answer yes-or-no questions with a probability. Think of a doctor deciding whether a patient has a certain illness, using two measurements such as temperature and heart rate. Past patients are dots on a chart: one colour for those who were ill, another for those who were not. Logistic regression draws a straight line across the chart to separate the two colours as well as it can. A new patient far on one side of the line gets a confident answer, such as nine chances in ten of being ill. A patient right on the line gets fifty-fifty. Close to the line the answer is unsure, which is honest. The computer finds the line by starting with a poor one. It checks how wrong its probabilities are for the patients it already knows about, shifts the line a little to be less wrong, and repeats. The method can only draw a straight line. If the two colours cannot be split that way, it does a poor job.
logistic-regression.analogyTitle: A ramp between a plain and a plateau
logistic-regression.analogyText: Picture the chart as a landscape seen from above. Along one straight line the ground is at exactly half height. On one side it rises smoothly to a plateau at height 1, and on the other it falls smoothly to a plain at height 0. The height at any spot is the model's probability that a patient there is ill. Training turns the ramp, slides it and makes it steeper, until the patients known to be ill stand on high ground and those known to be well stand on low ground.
logistic-regression.limits: This ramp has the same profile all the way along, so its contour lines are straight and parallel. A real pattern may need a boundary that curves or closes on itself, which no turning or sliding of a straight ramp can produce. The height is also only the model's belief. It matches real frequencies only when a straight ramp is a fair description of the data. And if the two groups can be separated perfectly, training never finishes shaping the ramp: it keeps steepening it toward a cliff.

decision-tree.simple: A decision tree is a list of yes-or-no questions, asked in order, that ends in a prediction. Think of a phone company that wants to know which customers are about to leave. It has records of past customers: how long each had been with the company, how often each rang to complain, and whether they left. The computer looks for the single question that best sorts those records into leavers and stayers. Perhaps it is: did they complain more than twice? No question sorts perfectly, so each of the two groups gets a question of its own, and so on. Drawn on paper, the questions branch like an upside-down tree. To predict for a new customer, start at the top and follow the answers down. The path also tells you why, because the reasons are the answers along the way. There is one trap. Keep adding questions and the tree ends up memorizing the old customers, quirks and all. Then it predicts new customers worse, not better.
decision-tree.analogyTitle: The key at the front of a field guide
decision-tree.analogyText: Many field guides open with a key. Are the leaves needles or flat? If needles, do they grow in bundles? Each answer sends you to another question until you arrive at a name. A decision tree is a key of exactly that kind, with one difference: nobody wrote it. The computer built it from a pile of specimens that were already named, by choosing at each step the question that separated them best.
decision-tree.limits: A botanist writes a key from an understanding of plants, and it holds for every specimen of the species. A learned tree knows only the specimens it was shown, and a different pile could give a different key. The botanist can plan the whole key at once, while the tree is built one question at a time by a simple score that never looks ahead. The questions are also narrower than a botanist's: each asks whether one number is above or below a value. Finally, a key ends in a certain name. A leaf of a learned tree ends in a majority, and some of the specimens that reached it may have been something else.

perceptron.simple: A perceptron is a simple machine for sorting things into two groups, and it learns from its own mistakes. Picture a table with apples and oranges scattered across it and a ruler lying on the table. The rule is that everything on one side of the ruler is called an apple, and everything on the other side an orange. At first the ruler is in a poor position. So you check the fruit one at a time. If a fruit is on the correct side, you do nothing. If it is on the wrong side, you shift the ruler toward it, enough to give that fruit a better chance next time. Then you move on to the next fruit, and go round the table again and again. If a straight ruler can separate the fruit at all, this routine is certain to find a position that gets every one right, and then it stops. If no such position exists, it never stops fiddling. The perceptron began as a model of a single brain cell, and today's neural networks are built from units much like it.
perceptron.analogyText: Watch what a single nudge of the ruler does. It shifts and turns the ruler toward one fruit that was on the wrong side, and it takes no account of any other fruit. So a nudge that helps one fruit can push another, previously correct, onto the wrong side, to be put right on a later round. That is why the ruler has to go round the table several times. The routine also stops at the first position that gets every fruit right, even if the ruler ends up brushing against a fruit when there was room to sit comfortably between the two groups.
perceptron.limits: The ruler is nearly the real thing: with two measurements for each fruit, the perceptron's boundary is a straight line. One detail the picture leaves vague is the size of each nudge, which is fixed by where the offending fruit sits, not by how wrong the ruler is. And a ruler is straight. If the two kinds of fruit can only be separated by a curve, you will go round the table for ever.

backpropagation.simple: Backpropagation is how a neural network finds out which of its settings to blame for a mistake. A neural network is a chain of simple calculations with many adjustable numbers, called weights. It makes a guess, and the guess is compared with the right answer. Usually the guess is somewhat wrong. The hard question is which weights to change, and by how much, when there may be millions of them. Think of a factory line where each worker passes a part to the next. A faulty product comes out at the end. The inspector tells the last worker what was wrong. That worker works out how much was their own doing and how much came from the part they were handed, and passes that message back. So it goes, worker by worker, to the start of the line. Backpropagation does this with numbers. It runs the network forwards to get the guess, then sends the error backwards, and every weight learns which way to move. The network nudges each weight a little and tries again.
backpropagation.analogyTitle: Tracing a fault back along a production line
backpropagation.analogyText: There is a slow way to assign blame on the factory line. Change one worker's setting a little, run the whole line again, and see whether the product improves. Then do the same for the next worker, and the next. With millions of workers that is millions of runs. The message passed back from the inspector does the job in a single trip. Each worker needs only the message from the worker after them. From it they work out how their own setting contributed, and how much of the fault was already in the part when it arrived, and they hand that second figure on. One run forwards and one message back, and everyone knows.
backpropagation.limits: Workers use judgment. Backpropagation uses one rule of calculus, applied mechanically, and its messages are exact rates of change that hold only for very small adjustments. In a network each unit also feeds many others, so blame comes back along many paths at once and has to be added up. And the message alone changes nothing. Deciding how far to move each setting is a separate step, done by gradient descent.

convolution.simple: A picture on a screen is a grid of tiny squares called pixels. Each pixel is stored as a number that says how bright it is. Convolution makes a new picture from an old one with the help of a small grid of numbers called a kernel. Lay the kernel over one patch of the picture. Multiply each pixel in the patch by the kernel number lying on top of it. Add up the results. That single sum becomes one pixel of the new picture. Then slide the kernel one step along and do it again, until it has visited every patch. Different kernels do different jobs. If all the kernel numbers are equal, each new pixel is an average of its neighbours, and the picture turns blurry. If one side of the kernel is negative and the other side positive, the sum is zero where the picture is smooth and large where the brightness changes suddenly. Those sudden changes are edges: the outlines of things.
convolution.analogyText: Take a card with a three by three block of windows cut in it, and write a number beside each window. Lay the card on a page covered in numbers, multiply what shows through each window by the number beside it, add up the nine products, and write the total on a second sheet at the matching place. Then slide the card one square and repeat. Think of the numbers on the card as what the card responds to. A card with negative numbers down one side and positive numbers down the other gives a total far from zero where the numbers on the page rise from one side of the patch to the other, and a total of zero where the page is flat. The second sheet then becomes a map of where that kind of change was found.
convolution.limits: The card hides a choice about the border, where it would hang off the page. Here the card simply never goes there, so the second sheet comes out smaller. And a card finds only its own pattern. An edge card says where brightness changes. It does not know whether the edge belongs to a face or a shadow.

graph-neural-network.simple: Some things are best described as a network: people and their friendships, towns and the roads between them, atoms and the bonds that hold a molecule together. A network like this is called a graph. Each thing is a node, and each link is an edge. A graph neural network is a way for a computer to work out something about each node by letting the nodes talk to their neighbours. Every node starts with a few numbers that describe it. Then comes a round of message passing. Each node collects its neighbours' numbers, averages them, and mixes that average with its own numbers by a fixed recipe. All the nodes do this at the same moment, and all of them use the same recipe. Each round carries what a node knows one link further. The recipe contains adjustable numbers called weights. Training means trying many examples and nudging the weights until the final numbers give good answers.
graph-neural-network.analogyText: Picture a village in which each household talks only to the houses next door. Once a day, at the same hour, every household asks its neighbours what they wrote in their notebooks yesterday, averages what it hears, and writes a new entry that mixes that average with its own last entry. News from next door arrives in one day. News from two doors away takes two days, because it first has to be written into the notebook in between. After a week, each notebook reflects everything within seven houses and nothing beyond.
graph-neural-network.limits: Villagers remember who told them what and can ask follow-up questions. A node only gets an average, so it cannot tell which neighbour said what, or even how many neighbours it has. Real gossip also keeps travelling for as long as people talk, while a graph neural network runs a small fixed number of rounds, so news from far away never arrives at all.

attention.simple: Attention is a way for each word in a sentence to collect information from the other words. Take the sentence: the cat sat on the mat because it was tired. To know what "it" means, you look back at "cat". A computer needs a way to do the same. In attention, every word sends out a question, and every word also wears a label saying what it has to offer. Questions, labels and everything else are lists of numbers. The computer compares one word's question with every word's label and gives each pair a score. A high score means: this word matters to that one. The scores are then turned into shares that add up to one whole, like slices of a pie. The word takes a blend of what the other words carry, with the biggest slices coming from the highest scores. Every word does this at once, so every word ends up knowing something about its sentence. A transformer is a program built by repeating this step many times, with other steps in between. The language models behind chatbots are transformers. Nobody writes their questions and labels by hand. They are found by training on enormous amounts of text.
attention.analogyTitle: A room where everyone compares notes
attention.analogyText: Picture a room of people, each holding three cards. The first card is a question: the kind of thing this person wants to know. The second is a badge, worn where everyone can see it, saying what this person knows about. The third is a page of notes, and it is the only card that changes hands. The badge is there to be matched against questions. The notes are what a good match earns. Each person compares their question with every badge in the room, their own included, then collects notes from everyone, taking a large share from the people whose badges matched well and a small share from the rest. Everyone leaves with a new page that mixes what the room knew, tilted towards what they asked about.
attention.limits: People would ask one or two others and ignore the rest. Attention takes a share from everyone it is allowed to see, and no share is ever exactly zero, only small. The cards are lists of numbers, a match is a sum of products, and nothing in the room understands anything. And because the questions and badges of a trained model were set by training, not written by anyone, it is often hard to say in words what a particular question is asking.

ddpm.simple: A diffusion model makes pictures by learning to undo damage. Take a clear photo and sprinkle a little random speckle over it, like static on an old television. Do it again, and again. After many rounds nothing is left but static. That direction is easy and needs no cleverness. Now imagine a program that has watched this happen to millions of pictures. It learns to look at a speckled picture and guess what the clean one underneath was. To make a brand new picture, start from pure static. Ask the program for its guess, and use it to wipe away a little of the speckle. Then ask again. Step by step, shapes come out of the static. The starting static is different every time, so the finished picture is different every time. The demonstration on this page is open about one limit. Its guesser is a plain formula that knows only four tiny pictures by heart, so those four are all it can ever produce.
ddpm.analogyTitle: A drop of ink in water, played backwards
ddpm.analogyText: Let a drop of ink fall into a glass of water. At first it is a sharp, intricate shape. Random jostling of the water spreads it out, and after a while the glass is an even grey with no trace of the shape. Film this and play it backwards: an even grey gathers itself into a drop. A diffusion model learns what one step of that backwards film looks like. Given a slightly-too-blurry frame, it produces a slightly sharper one. Starting from plain grey and applying that step many times, it arrives at a drop.
ddpm.limits: Real diffusion cannot be run backwards, and the model does not recover any particular drop that once existed. It makes up a plausible one, and a different one every time, because the grey it starts from is fresh random noise. Ink also spreads by moving through space, while the model's noise is added to each pixel separately and nothing moves. And the picture leaves out the hard part: the backwards step is not a law of nature here. It has to be learned from examples, and the result is only as good as that learning.

monte-carlo.simple: Monte Carlo estimation answers a hard question by trying random cases and counting. Suppose you want to know the area of an oddly shaped pond in a square field. Measuring it directly is difficult. Instead, throw a thousand pebbles into the field without aiming, so they land everywhere equally often. Then count how many splashed. If about three in every ten pebbles hit the water, the pond covers about three tenths of the field. No geometry was needed, only counting. More pebbles give a better answer, though the improvement is slow. To get an answer ten times closer, you need about a hundred times as many pebbles. Computers are good at this, because they can produce millions of random numbers in a second. Scientists use the same trick when a problem has too many possibilities to work through one by one, such as how light bounces around a room, or what a risky investment might be worth next year.
monte-carlo.analogyText: To learn what a country of millions thinks, a pollster does not ask everyone. They ask about a thousand people chosen at random and report the fraction who said yes. The answer is usually within a few percentage points of the truth, and the size of the country hardly matters: what matters is the size of the sample. Monte Carlo estimation polls the possibilities of a mathematical problem in the same way.
monte-carlo.limits: A pollster's hard problem is reaching a fair sample of people, and people can refuse or change their minds. A computer has neither difficulty with points in a square. Its difficulties are different. Its random numbers come from a formula and only imitate chance. And for many real problems, drawing fair samples is itself hard, which is why more advanced sampling methods exist.

bayesian-updating.simple: Bayesian updating is a rule for changing your mind by the right amount when you learn something new. Imagine a friend hands you a coin and warns you it might be a trick coin. Before any flips you already have an opinion. Perhaps you think it is probably fair. Then you flip it. One head tells you very little, so your opinion should barely move. Eight heads in ten flips is harder to shrug off. Eighty heads in a hundred flips should convince almost anyone. The rule says exactly how far to shift after each flip. Start from what you believed. Ask how well each possibility explains what you just saw. Possibilities that explain it well gain strength, and the others lose strength. Two things follow. Strong evidence moves you further than weak evidence. And the more firmly you believed something at the start, the more evidence it takes to change your mind. Doctors reading test results and email filters deciding what is spam both reason this way.
bayesian-updating.analogyText: A detective starts a case with some suspects more likely than others. Each clue shifts suspicion toward the suspects who would more probably have left it. Mud on the carpet points to anyone who came through the garden, a little. A fingerprint points to one person, a lot. No single ordinary clue settles the case, but they accumulate, and a suspect who started out unlikely needs stronger clues before the detective accuses them.
bayesian-updating.limits: A detective weighs clues by feel, and the rule needs numbers: how likely each suspect was at the start, and how probable each clue would be if they were guilty. Those numbers can be hard to justify, and two honest people may choose different ones. The rule also only shares belief out among the suspects on the list. If the culprit was never listed, no amount of evidence will name them.

ab-testing.simple: An A/B test is a fair race between two versions of something. A shop wants to know whether a green Buy button sells more than its blue one. So each visitor is shown one of the two, chosen by a coin flip. After a while the shop counts. Say 10 in every 100 bought with blue, and 12 in every 100 bought with green. Is green better? Maybe. But two groups of people never behave exactly alike, even when they see the very same page. Some gap always appears by luck. So the test asks one question. If the buttons were really the same, how often would luck alone make a gap this big? If the answer is "hardly ever", the shop trusts the gap. If the answer is "quite often", it has learned nothing yet and needs more visitors. One rule is easy to break. Decide how many visitors to wait for before you start, and then wait. If you keep checking and stop the moment green is ahead, luck will fool you far more often.
ab-testing.analogyText: You want to know whether two bags of flour weigh the same, but your scale is twitchy: weigh the same bag twice and it reads a little differently each time. One reading of each bag settles nothing. So you first learn how much the scale twitches, and then ask whether the two bags differ by clearly more than a twitch. An A/B test does this with people in place of flour. The twitch is the luck of who happened to visit. The test works out how big that twitch is for the number of visitors you had, and it calls a difference real only when the gap is about twice the twitch or more.
ab-testing.limits: You can weigh the same bag again, but you cannot show the same visitor both pages as if for the first time. The test has to compare two different groups and rely on chance to make them alike. A scale twitches by the same amount every day, while visitors change with the hour, the weekday and the season. And a scale tells you how much heavier a bag is, whereas the test on its own says only whether a difference probably exists, not whether it is large enough to matter.

exponential-smoothing.simple: Exponential smoothing is a way to estimate next month's number from the months before. Picture a bakery deciding how many loaves to bake. Last month it sold 120. In the months before that it sold about 100. Which number should it trust? The newest one is the freshest news, but it might be a fluke. The older ones are steadier, but things may have changed since. Exponential smoothing takes a middle path. It keeps one running estimate. Each month it compares the estimate with what really happened, and moves the estimate part of the way toward the real figure. A small move ignores flukes but is slow to notice a real change. A big move reacts fast but gets pushed around by every odd month. Recent months end up counting most, and older months fade bit by bit. Two add-ons make it more useful. One keeps track of whether sales are climbing or falling. The other remembers which months of the year are always busy, like December in a toy shop.
exponential-smoothing.analogyText: You've eaten at a restaurant many times and have a settled opinion of it. Tonight, the meal is unusually bad. You don't decide the restaurant is terrible, but you don't ignore the experience either. Your opinion drops a little. If the next few meals are bad too, your opinion keeps falling until it reflects what the kitchen is serving now. Older meals still influence your view, but less and less as time passes. Exponential smoothing treats demand in much the same way: your opinion is its running estimate, and each meal is a new month's figure.
exponential-smoothing.limits:
Your opinion changes by instinct. Exponential smoothing changes its estimate by a precise fraction, controlled by a setting called the smoothing weight. This is the size of the move described above: small for a steady estimate, large for a quick one. The best setting depends on the data and can be found by testing different values and measuring how well they forecast.

You might also know why tonight's meal was bad: perhaps the usual chef was away. The method knows nothing about the reasons behind the numbers. It cannot tell whether a poor result is a one-off or the start of a lasting change until later observations provide more evidence.

reservoir-sampling.simple: Reservoir sampling picks a fair random handful from a stream of things when you do not know how long the stream will be. Imagine watching a parade with room in your notebook for only three names. Marchers pass one at a time, and nobody will tell you how many are coming. You want every marcher to have the same chance of ending up in your notebook. Writing down the first three would be unfair to everyone after them. Here is the trick. Write down the first three. When the fourth marcher passes, give them a three in four chance of replacing a name chosen at random from your notebook. Give the fifth marcher a three in five chance, the sixth a three in six chance, and so on. Later marchers are less likely to get in. But earlier names have faced more chances of being pushed out. The two effects balance exactly. Whenever the parade ends, every marcher has had the same chance.
reservoir-sampling.analogyTitle: Choosing one song from the radio
reservoir-sampling.analogyText: You decide to remember one song from tonight's radio show, chosen fairly, without knowing how many songs will play. Remember the first song. When the second plays, flip a coin to decide whether to switch to it. When the third plays, switch with a chance of one in three. Stop there and check. The third song is the one you hold one time in three. Each of the first two won the coin flip half the time and then survived the third song two times in three, which also comes to one in three. The same balance holds at the tenth song, with a chance of one in ten, and at whatever moment the show ends.
reservoir-sampling.limits: This is the case of a sample of one. Keeping several items needs the extra step of choosing which held item to replace. And a fair chance is not the same as a representative result: a sample of one song says little about the whole show.

metropolis-hastings.simple: Metropolis-Hastings is a way to explore a landscape in proportion to its height, when you can only measure the height where you stand. Imagine a hiker wandering through hills in fog. She wants to spend most of her time on high ground, and exactly twice as long at places that are twice as high. She has an altimeter but no map. So she follows a simple rule. Pick a random spot nearby and check its height. If it is higher, go there. If it is lower, go there only sometimes: half the time if it is half as high, one time in ten if it is a tenth as high. Otherwise stay put, and write down the place where she is standing once more. Keep a list of everywhere she stood. Over a long walk, that list traces the shape of the whole landscape. Scientists use this to study things they can score but cannot list in full, such as every arrangement of the atoms in a liquid, or every explanation that fits a set of measurements.
metropolis-hastings.analogyTitle: A politician touring a chain of islands
metropolis-hastings.analogyText: A politician wants to spend time on each island of a long chain in proportion to its population, but has no list of populations. Each day they consider moving to a randomly chosen neighbouring island and ask the two mayors for their populations. If the neighbour is larger, they go. If it is smaller, they go with probability equal to the ratio of the populations, and otherwise stay another day. Two numbers a day are all the politician ever learns, and only their ratio is used. Yet after many days, the number of days spent on each island is proportional to its population.
metropolis-hastings.limits: The islands are few and in a line. Real problems have a continuum of positions in many dimensions, where choosing a good size and direction for the proposed move is the hard part. The story also hides two facts. Successive days are not independent: where the politician is today depends on yesterday, so a week of days is worth far less than seven independent draws. And if two groups of islands are separated by a long stretch of empty ones, the politician may never cross, and nothing in the daily record would reveal that half the population was missed.

kalman-filter.simple: A Kalman filter keeps track of something that moves when your measurements of it are shaky. Think of following a friend's car on a phone map. The dot jumps around, because satellite positioning is never exact. But you know something else as well: a car on a road moves smoothly. A second ago it was there, driving that way at that speed, so now it should be about here. The filter blends these two sources. First it predicts where the car should be now. Then it looks at the new measurement and moves its guess part of the way toward it. How far? That depends on which source deserves more trust. If the measurements are poor, it leans on the prediction. If the prediction is doubtful, it leans on the measurement. It also keeps a running score of how unsure it is, and updates that score at every step. The result is a steadier and more accurate track than the raw measurements give.
kalman-filter.analogyTitle: A navigator with a compass and a glimpse of the coast
kalman-filter.analogyText: A ship's navigator without satellite positioning keeps a running estimate of the ship's position from its speed and heading. This is dead reckoning, and its error grows with every hour. Now and then the navigator sights a lighthouse and gets a position fix, which has its own error. A good navigator does not jump to the fix or ignore it, but moves the plotted position toward it by an amount that depends on how much each is trusted. After hours of dead reckoning, a fix counts for a lot. Just after a good fix, the next rough sighting counts for little.
kalman-filter.limits: A navigator weighs things by judgement. The filter uses exact formulas that are only as good as the noise levels it is given. Tell it the sensor is better than it really is and it will follow the noise. The formulas also assume that errors are bell-shaped and that the motion follows a linear rule. A navigator can reason that the ship cannot be on land. The basic filter cannot represent a fact like that.

particle-filter.simple: A particle filter keeps track of something it cannot see directly by making many guesses at once. Picture a robot in a long hallway that has lost its place. It could be in several spots, so the filter scatters a few hundred guesses along the hallway. Each guess is called a particle, and each one says, "maybe the robot is here". Then three things happen, again and again. First, when the robot drives forward, every guess is moved forward too, with a small random nudge because wheels slip. Second, the robot's sensor takes a reading and each guess is scored. A guess that would have produced that reading scores high. A guess that would not scores low. Third, the filter makes a fresh set of guesses by copying the high scorers and dropping the low ones. After a few rounds the guesses crowd around the place where the robot really is. Because the guesses can sit in several places at once, the filter can stay undecided between two spots until the readings settle the matter.
particle-filter.analogyTitle: A search party with one radio
particle-filter.analogyText: A hiker is lost on a moor, and the search party has only so many people. They spread out over every place she might be. Then a report comes over the radio: her phone was heard about two kilometres from the mast. That does not say where she is, but it says where she is not. Searchers standing about two kilometres from the mast are in promising places. Searchers anywhere else are wasting their time, so they walk over and join the promising ones. As the hiker moves, the searchers drift the way she is likely to drift. With each new report the party thins out in the wrong places and thickens in the right ones.
particle-filter.limits: Real searchers can look around, think and change the plan. A particle does nothing but hold a position. Real searchers who find nothing widen the search, while the basic filter can only copy the particles it already has: if none of them is near the truth, no amount of copying will put one there.

rrt.simple: A rapidly-exploring random tree, or RRT, finds a way for a robot to get from one place to another without bumping into things. It works a little like a plant growing through a garden full of rocks. The plant starts as a single shoot at the robot's starting point. Again and again, the planner picks a random spot somewhere on the map. It finds the part of the plant that is closest to that spot and grows a short new twig from there toward it. If the twig would poke through a rock, it is thrown away. Otherwise it stays. Random spots are scattered all over the map, so the plant is pulled outward in every direction and soon reaches into every open area. When a twig comes close enough to the goal, the planner follows the plant back from that twig to the root. That chain of twigs is a route the robot can follow. The route is usually crooked. It is the first one found, not the shortest.
rrt.analogyText: A team is exploring an unmapped island from a base camp. A dispatcher, who cannot see the terrain, keeps calling out random map coordinates. Each time, the camp nearest to those coordinates sends a scout a short walk in that direction. If the way is clear, the scout sets up a new camp there. If a cliff is in the way, the scout turns back. Now ask which camps answer most of the calls. While most of the island is unexplored, most coordinates fall far from every camp, and the camp nearest to a far-off point is one on the edge of the explored area. The edge camps do most of the sending, which is why the camps spread quickly across the whole island instead of crowding around the base.
rrt.limits: Real scouts would learn from a cliff and walk around it. The algorithm learns nothing from a failed branch and may try the same wall many times. A real robot's position is often a list of joint angles and not a place on a map, and its obstacles in that space are invisible shapes known only through a yes-or-no collision test.

run-length-encoding.simple: Run-length encoding is a way to write repeated things in less space. Suppose you are reading a row of floor tiles aloud to a friend: white, white, white, white, white, white, black, black. You would soon stop naming each tile. You would say "six white, then two black" instead. That is the whole idea. A run is a stretch of the same thing repeated, with nothing else in between. Run-length encoding replaces every run with two pieces of information: how many, and of what. Your friend can rebuild the row exactly, tile for tile, so nothing is lost. This saves a lot of space when the data has long runs, like a drawing with large areas of one colour. It does not help with ordinary writing, where a letter is rarely followed by the same letter. There it makes things longer, because every single letter now needs its own count.
run-length-encoding.analogyText: A knitting pattern does not list every stitch. It says "knit 6, purl 2, knit 6". The knitter reads a count and a kind of stitch, and produces exactly the row the designer meant. Run-length encoding writes data the same way: a count, then the thing to repeat.
run-length-encoding.limits: A designer chooses rows with long repeats. Data does not cooperate like that. The picture also hides a cost. A person reads "6" without thinking about the room it takes, but in a file the count occupies space of its own: 8 bits for every run in this lesson.

huffman-coding.simple: Huffman coding is a way to write a message using as few 0s and 1s as possible. A computer stores every letter as a pattern of 0s and 1s, and normally every letter gets a pattern of the same length. That is wasteful, because some letters turn up far more often than others. In English, e is everywhere and z is rare. Huffman coding gives short patterns to the common letters and longer patterns to the rare ones. There is one more requirement. The patterns must be chosen so that the message can be read back without any gaps between letters. For that, no pattern may be the beginning of another pattern. Huffman coding finds such a set by tying the two rarest letters together, treating the pair as one, and repeating until everything is joined into a single tree. For that message, no other set of patterns of this kind is shorter.
huffman-coding.analogyTitle: Morse code, with the gaps removed
huffman-coding.analogyText: Morse code gives the commonest English letters the shortest signals: E is one dot and T is one dash, while Q is dash dash dot dash. A telegraph operator therefore sends fewer signals for ordinary text than a code with equal-length letters would need. Huffman coding follows the same principle, short for common and long for rare, and works out the best lengths from actual counts.
huffman-coding.limits: Morse code cannot be read as an unbroken stream. One dot is E, and it is also the start of A (dot dash), so the operator must leave a silence between letters. That silence is a third signal. A Huffman code needs no silences, because no code is the beginning of another. Morse code was also fixed once for all English text, while a Huffman code is computed for one particular set of counts and is only the best code for those counts.

lz77.simple: LZ77 is a way to make a text shorter by not writing the same thing twice. Think about how people write. Words and phrases come back again and again. LZ77 takes advantage of that. It reads the text from start to finish. At each point it looks back over the last stretch it has read and asks: have I seen what comes next before? If so, it does not write those letters again. It writes a short note instead: go back this far, and copy this many letters. If not, it writes the letter as it is. Someone holding the notes can rebuild the whole text, because every note points to something already rebuilt. The more a text repeats itself, the shorter it gets. A text with no repeats gets longer, because each note takes up room too.
lz77.analogyTitle: A song sheet that says "repeat chorus"
lz77.analogyText: A printed song does not spell out the chorus after every verse. It prints the chorus once and afterwards writes "repeat chorus". The singer looks back up the page, finds the words and sings them again. LZ77 writes that kind of instruction for every repeat it can find: look back this far, and copy this much.
lz77.limits: A songwriter knows where the chorus is and gives it a name. LZ77 has no names. It can only point backwards by distance, and only as far as its window reaches, so a phrase that returns after a long gap is not found. It also matches exact symbols only: a chorus with one changed word is copied up to the change and no further. And every instruction costs bits, so copying one or two letters usually costs more than writing them out.

byte-pair-encoding.simple: Byte-pair encoding is a way to chop text into pieces that a computer can treat as single units. Whole words make poor pieces. There are too many of them, and new ones keep turning up. Single letters make poor pieces too. There are only a few, but every text becomes a very long string of them. Byte-pair encoding finds pieces in between. It starts with the text split into single letters. Then it looks for the two neighbouring pieces that occur together most often, such as t next to h, and glues them into one new piece, th. It writes that rule down and looks again. After many rounds the common words have become single pieces. Rarer words are built from a few familiar chunks, the way slowest is slow plus est. Any new word can then be split by replaying the same rules in the same order. The pieces are called tokens. Language models, including the ones behind chatbots, read and write text as tokens made in this way or a similar one.
byte-pair-encoding.analogyText: Someone copying out a long document by hand notices that they keep writing the same two marks side by side. They invent one new mark for the pair and note it in a legend at the top of the page: "this mark means t then h". Later they notice the new mark often sits next to e, so they invent another mark for that, defined in terms of the first. The legend grows one line at a time, and each line may use marks defined above it. Anyone holding the legend can copy out new documents in the same shorthand, and can expand the shorthand back into the original letters.
byte-pair-encoding.limits: A person would invent shorthand for units that mean something. Byte-pair encoding follows the counts wherever they lead, so its pieces can cut across meaning. A person might also revise the legend later. Here a rule, once made, is never reconsidered, and the legend depends entirely on the one text it was built from. And when two pairs are equally common a person would use judgment, while the method needs a fixed tie rule so that everyone who repeats the work gets the same legend.

diffie-hellman.simple: Diffie-Hellman key exchange lets two people agree on a secret number while everyone else is listening. That sounds impossible. If Alice and Bob have never met, and a stranger hears every word they say, how can they end up sharing a secret? The answer is a kind of arithmetic that is easy to do and very hard to undo. Alice and Bob each pick a private number and keep it to themselves. Each one scrambles a public starting number using their private number, and sends the result. Then each scrambles what they received, using their own private number again. Both arrive at the same final number. The listener saw the two scrambled results, but cannot work backwards to either private number, so cannot reach the final one. That final number becomes the key that locks the rest of the conversation. On this page the numbers are tiny so that you can follow every step. Numbers this small are easy to crack. They are for learning only and protect nothing.
diffie-hellman.analogyText: Alice and Bob agree, in the open, on a common paint colour, say yellow. Each secretly chooses a private colour. Each mixes their private colour into some yellow and sends the mixture to the other, where anyone can see it. Then each stirs their own private colour into the mixture they received. Both now hold yellow plus Alice's colour plus Bob's colour, the same final shade. A spy saw yellow and the two mixtures. Separating a mixture back into its ingredients is impractical, and without one of the private colours she cannot make the final shade.
diffie-hellman.limits: Paint is only a picture of "easy to do, hard to undo". Un-mixing paint is hard for physical reasons. Undoing the arithmetic is hard only as far as anyone knows: for large, well-chosen numbers no fast method has been found, but nobody has proved that none exists, and a large quantum computer could do it. With small numbers, like the ones on this page, it is easy. The picture also says nothing about who you are mixing with. If someone sits in the middle and swaps the tins, Alice and Bob each end up sharing a colour with that person instead of with each other. The real protocol has exactly this weakness unless the messages are also signed.

rsa.simple: RSA is a way to send a secret to someone you have never met, without agreeing on a password first. Picture a padlock that anyone can snap shut but only one key can open. The receiver hands out open padlocks to everybody and keeps the key at home. To send a secret, you put it in a box, snap a padlock on it and post it. Not even you can open it again. Only the receiver can. RSA builds this padlock out of numbers. The receiver secretly picks two prime numbers, which are numbers such as 7 or 13 that nothing divides evenly except 1 and themselves. Multiplying the two primes gives a number that is made public. It acts as the padlock. The primes themselves stay secret and act as the key. Multiplying two primes is quick. Finding them again from the answer is extremely slow when the primes are hundreds of digits long. On this page the primes are tiny, so that you can follow every step. Numbers this small can be cracked at once. They are for learning only, and you should never build your own version to protect anything real.
rsa.analogyTitle: Why the padlock can be given away
rsa.analogyText: The padlock is safe to hand out for one reason. Snapping it shut is something anyone can do, and doing it teaches you nothing about how to open it. Closing and opening are different acts, and only opening needs the key. That is the property RSA has to build out of numbers: a calculation that anyone can perform with the public number, and that, as far as anyone knows, can be reversed in practice only by someone who knows the secret primes. It is also why the sender, having locked the box, cannot open it again.
rsa.limits: A steel padlock is opened by cutting it. The RSA padlock is opened by arithmetic: anyone who can split the public number into its two primes can make the key. Nobody has proved that this splitting must be slow, and a large enough quantum computer could do it quickly. A padlock also behaves the same way every time, and for a padlock that is fine. For RSA it is a weakness: locking the same message twice gives the same result, so a spy who can guess the message can lock her guess and compare. Real systems mix random padding into the message before locking it. The picture also leaves out how a sender knows the padlock really belongs to the receiver, which needs certificates.

bresenham-line.simple: A screen is a grid of tiny squares called pixels. Each pixel is either lit or dark. So how do you draw a slanted line? You cannot light half a pixel. You have to choose whole pixels that sit as close to the true line as they can. Bresenham's algorithm chooses them one at a time. It walks from one end of the line to the other, one column per step. At each step there are only two choices: stay in the same row, or move over by one row. To decide, it keeps one running number. That number says how far the chosen pixels have drifted from the true line. When the drift passes half a pixel, the walk moves over a row and the number drops back. The number is always a whole number, with no fractions. So the method only needs to add, subtract and compare, which even a very basic computer chip does quickly.
bresenham-line.analogyText: Picture a long, gentle ramp, and a supply of square blocks that you stack beside it so the block tops follow the ramp as closely as blocks can. Walk along the ramp one block-width at a time. At each stop, look at the gap between the ramp and the top of your stack. If the ramp has climbed more than half a block above the stack, add one block. Otherwise leave the stack alone. You never measure the ramp from the ground again. You only keep track of the gap, and the gap changes by the same amount at every stop.
bresenham-line.limits: A person would measure the gap with a ruler and get fractions. The algorithm avoids that: it scales everything by a fixed whole number first, so the quantity it tracks is always a whole number, and it compares against zero instead of against half a block. The ramp also only climbs gently to the right. Real lines can head in any direction, including steeper than 45 degrees, where the algorithm must walk row by row instead of column by column.

graham-scan.simple: Hammer some nails into a board. Now stretch a rubber band around all of them and let go. It snaps tight against the outermost nails and ignores the rest. That outline is called the convex hull. Convex means it has no dents. A computer has no rubber band, so it needs a method. Graham scan starts at the lowest nail, which must be on the outline. It then visits the other nails in order, sweeping around like a clock hand running backwards. It joins each nail to the one before, as if drawing the outline. After each new nail it checks the last corner it drew. If the path bends left there, fine. If it bends right, that corner is a dent, so the nail there cannot be on the outline. The nail is dropped, and the corner before it is checked again. When the sweep ends, the nails still kept are the corners of the rubber band's shape.
graham-scan.analogyText: Trace the stretched band with a finger, going counter-clockwise. At every nail it touches, the band bends the same way: to the left. It cannot bend to the right anywhere, because a right bend would be a dent, and a stretched band pulls every dent flat. Graham scan turns that observation into a test. It draws a path through the nails in sweeping order, and wherever the path bends right at a nail, that nail is one the band would never touch. Dropping it is the band pulling the dent flat.
graham-scan.limits: The band finds the whole outline at once, by physics. A computer has only a list of coordinates and must examine points a few at a time, which is why the sort and the stack are needed. A real band also rests against nails that happen to stand along a straight side, between two corners. This lesson's algorithm reports only the corners and leaves those out.

consistent-hashing.simple: Big websites keep their data on many computers, called servers. To fetch a piece of data, a program must know which server holds it. A simple rule is to number the servers and do a little arithmetic on the data's name. That rule has a flaw. Add or remove one server, and almost every piece of data is suddenly assigned somewhere else. Nearly everything would have to be copied to a new home. Consistent hashing avoids this. Imagine a circle, like a clock face. Each server is given a spot on the circle. Each piece of data is given a spot too. The data belongs to the first server you meet when you walk clockwise from its spot. Now add a new server. It takes over only the stretch of circle just behind it. The data on that stretch moves to the new server. Everything else stays exactly where it was.
consistent-hashing.analogyTitle: Stops on a circular bus route
consistent-hashing.analogyText: A road runs in a ring round a town, with houses all along it and a handful of bus stops. Everybody walks clockwise along the road to the first stop they come to. If the town builds a new stop, only the households between the previous stop and the new one change their habits: they now reach the new stop first. If a stop closes, only its own passengers are affected. They walk on to the next one. Nobody else in town notices.
consistent-hashing.limits: Houses and bus stops stand where they do for reasons. On a hash ring every position is a scrambled number with no meaning, and that scrambling is what spreads the keys evenly. Nobody walks, either: finding the next server is a quick search in a sorted list of positions. The picture also leaves out two things real systems add. Each server is given many positions, not one, so that the stretches even out. And each item is usually stored on several servers in a row, so that losing one server loses no data.

grovers-search.simple: Suppose you have a huge pile of keys and one lock. Only one key fits, and the only way to find out is to try a key in the lock. An ordinary computer tries keys one at a time. On average it gets through half the pile. Grover's search is a method for a quantum computer that needs far fewer tries: for a million keys, about eight hundred. It does not test every key at the same moment. The state of a quantum computer is described by a list of numbers, one for each key, called amplitudes. Nobody can read these numbers directly. When you look at the machine you see just one key, and a key with a bigger number is more likely to be the one you see. Each use of the lock test, followed by one fixed adjustment, makes the right key's number grow and the others shrink. After the right number of rounds, looking gives the right key almost every time. Quantum computers big enough to do this for a useful problem do not exist yet. This page uses an ordinary computer to work out the same numbers.
grovers-search.analogyTitle: Turning a dial in equal clicks
grovers-search.analogyText: Picture a dial with a pointer. Straight up means "certain to see the right answer". Flat means "certain to see a wrong one". At the start the pointer is almost flat, because the right answer is one among many. Each round of the algorithm turns the pointer upward by the same small angle. After enough rounds it points nearly straight up, and that is the moment to look. Keep turning and it swings past the top and back down, so extra rounds make things worse.
grovers-search.limits: There is no pointer inside the machine. The dial is a summary of a long list of amplitudes, and the turning comes from two operations that make some amplitudes add up and others cancel. Ordinary chances never cancel each other like that, which is why no everyday object behaves this way. You also cannot watch the dial. Looking at a quantum computer gives one answer and destroys the state, so the number of rounds has to be worked out beforehand. And the dial says nothing about cost. Each click needs the test to be built as a quantum circuit and run without errors, which is the hard part in practice.
